statement: In a systematic review of 48 studies (1,774 people) of psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT and mescaline, mostly given in laboratories, clinical trials or ceremonies with preparation and aftercare (Evens et al., 2023; AMSTAR 2 critically low), measurements taken between one day and one month after use, compared with each person's own measurements before, most often showed less depression and stress and more wellbeing, mindfulness and social connectedness (changes reported in 70 to 90% of the studies that measured these), and no study found group-level worsening of mental health. Bad after-effects were reported in 14 of the 25 studies that said they looked for them: mostly headaches (52 people, usually lasting a day or two), then sleep problems, tension and exhaustion, with single cases of severe anxiety and of relapse to methamphetamine use. Half the studies had a control group of some kind, but only 14 of the 48 had a placebo group with double-blinding, only statistically significant results were counted, and half the studies did not say whether they looked for side effects, so the size and cause of these changes, and how often they happen with recreational use, are unknown. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: A review of 48 studies found that in the days and weeks after taking a psychedelic, people often felt less depressed and stressed and more connected, compared with before. Some had headaches or slept badly, and a few had serious anxiety. Most studies had no comparison group and took place with support around them, so we do not know how big or how common these changes are in everyday use.
population: Adults, clinical and nonclinical, taking classic psychedelics in laboratory studies, clinical trials or ceremonies, in 48 studies gathered by a systematic review
exposure: A session with psilocybin, ayahuasca or DMT, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT or mescaline
comparator: The same people's measurements before the session (a control group in 24 studies, placebo-controlled and double-blind in 14)
outcome: Psychological measures and adverse effects between one day and one month after use
magnitude: No effect sizes; counts of studies. Changes in 70 to 90% of studies measuring depression, stress and grief; mindfulness; personality and attitudes; wellbeing; social effects. Adverse events: assessed or mentioned in 25 of 48 studies (550 participants); none in 11 (297 participants); reported in 14 (253 participants): 52 headaches, 6 sleep disturbances, 6 tension, 3 exhaustion, 3 visual distortion, single severe cases.

statement: In adults who planned, on their own initiative, to take a classic psychedelic, a better state of mind measured before the drug is associated with a less challenging experience, and in laboratory LSD sessions mood and personality measured before the dose were associated with how the session went; many of the larger associations reported come from people recalling afterwards how they had felt. In the only prospective study outside a laboratory among these sources (Haijen et al., 2018; self-selected adults who answered online surveys; of the 379 who reported back, 48% took LSD or 1P-LSD, 29% psilocybin and 11% ayahuasca), feeling comfortable, open, well prepared, not anxious and in a good mood, rated by the participants within the day before ('set'), went with lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores they gave about a day after (standardized beta −0.32, SE 0.07; moderate in the editors' terms), as did recreational or social intentions rated a week before (−0.22; small). Strong expectations and a clear intention went with higher mystical-type (0.18) and visual (0.16) scores but not clearly with challenge, and set was unrelated to mystical-type scores. The trait absorption went with more intense experiences of every kind, challenging (0.22) as well as mystical-type (0.35), while trait anxiety, openness, emotional stability, suggestibility and the number of earlier psychedelic experiences showed no statistically significant association with any of them in this model of about 198 people. The sample shrank from 654 a week before to about 198 in this analysis (editors' inference), and the predictors were adjusted for one another and for an amount the participants estimated after the experience, not for the drug taken or psychiatric history. Average well-being rose from 49.0 before to 52.6 two weeks after, with no comparison group and fewer than half the sample remaining, and mystical-type scores no longer predicted it once traits, intentions, set and setting were in the model. In healthy volunteers given LSD, mostly lying in bed in a quiet hospital room and mostly with a placebo session for comparison (nine Basel laboratory studies, 213 people; Vizeli et al., 2024), higher well-being rated on a mood questionnaire before the dose went with stronger effects on every self-rated scale except a rating of a bad drug effect and two others, the anxiety scales included, so in these sessions a better mood went with a stronger experience rather than a less challenging one; anxiety rated before the dose went with more anxiety during the session, and openness with more mystical-type ratings, all at a given dose; the text gives no sizes. In two retrospective studies of people who had used psilocybin, as summarized by a systematic review the editors rate critically low (Aday et al., 2021), states recalled after the experience were associated with it; in the one for which the review gives figures (143 people), surrender correlated with mystical-type experience (r = 0.72) and preoccupation and confusion with dread (0.64 and 0.58). In a US online panel, people who blamed a negative mindset for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.14) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others afterwards (odds ratio 4.56, 95% CI 2.10 to 9.94, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any; Simonsson et al., 2023). Such recalled states are associations reported by the same people at the same sitting, not predictors. An opinion piece by the same research group as the prospective study (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) previewed, in one figure and without methods, preliminary models from what appears to be an earlier cut of the same online survey (266 people who completed four surveys): readiness, a clear intention with strong expectations, and trust in the people who would be present, all rated before the experience, went with less challenging experiences; because it gives no named outcome measures or full measurement details, sample description or model details and its sample appears to overlap the prospective study's, it is not counted as a further study and its figures are not used. Preparation is routine in clinical trials, but none of those reviewed compared different kinds of it: a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025; it mapped what the trials reported, without appraising them or combining their outcomes), found that 21 described giving information about the effects, 19 meetings beforehand to build trust (mostly one to four, of about 2 hours each) and 18 advice on the attitude to take, mostly openness and letting go, and that no included trial compared different preparation, sets or settings; the review's remark that one trial's two-interview preparation made the experience and its benefits greater rests on a trial that did not vary preparation. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: People who felt calm, open and ready the day before a trip they had planned rated it as less difficult. In laboratory LSD sessions, feeling anxious beforehand went with more anxiety, while feeling well went with stronger effects overall, not easier ones. These links come from watching, not testing, and many people dropped out of the study outside the laboratory. Studies in which people recalled their mood afterwards found bigger links, but memories can be coloured by how the trip went. Clinical trials prepare people with meetings and advice beforehand, but a review of 25 trials found none that compared different ways of preparing.
population: Adults who use classic psychedelics: people who planned a psychedelic experience on their own initiative and signed up online (one prospective study), healthy volunteers given LSD in laboratory studies, and people recalling past experiences in surveys
exposure: State of mind, intentions and traits measured before the drug (set within a day before; intentions and traits a week before; mood before a laboratory dose, personality at screening), and, in retrospective studies, states recalled afterwards
comparator: People with lower or higher scores on each measure within the same study; no study read here compared people helped to prepare with people who were not, and a systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials up to December 2023 found none that compared different preparation, sets or settings
outcome: How challenging, mystical-type or intense the experience was, self-rated (Challenging Experience Questionnaire, Mystical Experience Questionnaire, 5D-ASC, visual analogue scales), and well-being in the following weeks
magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018), standardized coefficients adjusted for one another and for self-estimated amount (about 198 people): set and challenging experience −0.32 (SE 0.07); recreational or social intentions −0.22 (SE 0.08); clear intentions and mystical-type 0.18, visual 0.16, challenging −0.13 (p = 0.088); absorption and challenging 0.22, mystical-type 0.35; R2 0.32 for challenging experience. Vizeli et al. (2024): directions and significance only (sizes are in a figure and a supplement not used): pre-dose well-being with stronger effects on all self-rated scales but three, the anxiety scales included; pre-dose anxiety with more anxiety during the session. Recalled afterwards: surrender r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, preoccupation 0.64 and confusion 0.58 with dread (n = 143, one of the two retrospective studies, as summarized by Aday et al., 2021); negative mindset blamed for the most challenging experience: beta 0.14, harm thoughts or attempts OR 4.56 (95% CI 2.10 to 9.94), adjusted only for the other attributions (Simonsson et al., 2023).

No review protocol, registration or formal trial quality/risk-of-bias appraisal is reported in the article. Each study was scored for reporting 16 set-and-setting sub-domains; the Methods states that no data synthesis was planned.

risk_of_bias.note: The prospective study is at high risk of bias (drug type, psychiatric history and other drugs not adjusted; the amount estimated after the experience; about 70% of the baseline sample not in the analysis; when the day-before survey was completed could not be confirmed, and it could be filled in on paper and entered later), the laboratory analysis has some concerns (each predictor adjusted for dose only; no sizes in the text), and the recalled-state findings are at very high risk (attributions made at the same sitting as the outcome) and are worded only as associations (cards sc_haijen_2018, sc_vizeli_2024, sc_aday_2021, sc_simonsson_2023).

inconsistency.note: More anxiety, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, measured before the drug went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in both the naturalistic and the laboratory source. In the laboratory a better general mood went with stronger effects overall, the anxiety scales included by the text, rather than with a less challenging session; that is a different mood scale and outcome from the naturalistic study's set component, so the claim states it instead of rating it as inconsistency (the certainty would stay very low either way). Absorption's link with mystical and challenging experience alike is reported, not a conflict.

indirectness.note: Worded for the populations studied (self-selected, mostly experienced people planning their own use; screened laboratory volunteers).

imprecision.note: The main prospective coefficient has a standard error of 0.07; for the laboratory analysis only directions are claimed.

publication_bias.note: The review admitted only predictors reported as significant, a file-drawer problem its authors name; the primary studies are cited directly and the review's figures are labelled as summarized.

grade.reasoning: Predictor studies start low, even inside randomized laboratory studies, because the predictors were not randomized; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated, for the direction only: more anxiety beforehand, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in two independent sources measured before the drug, one prospective and naturalistic (Imperial College London, the set component) and one laboratory (Basel, pre-dose anxiety), with different questionnaires, so it is a conceptual replication; recalled attributions in an independent panel (Simonsson et al.) point the same way. That a better mood goes with an easier experience rests on the naturalistic study alone: in the laboratory a better mood went with stronger effects overall. The other predictors rest on single studies or on states recalled afterwards. The review (Aday et al., 2021) is used only for what it adds (the retrospective Russ studies and the tabulation of absorption), since its Table 1 misprints the sign for set. Two further sources change neither the certainty nor the status: an opinion piece from the same group (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018), whose preliminary survey figure appears to come from an earlier cut of the prospective study's sample and gives no methods, is not counted as a further study or used for any figure (opinion pieces are not evidence for empirical claims, METHODS §3.2); and a systematic review of how 25 psychiatric trials reported set and setting (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; a map of reporting, not of effects) shows only that no such trial up to December 2023 compared preparation, sets or settings. A randomized study in 75 healthy volunteers that varied the amount of preparation together with the dose and the support afterwards (Griffiths et al., 2018) is known here only from its description by Strickland et al. (2021) and has not been read.

statement: In people who use classic psychedelics, feeling safe and supported is associated with fewer reported difficulties in retrospective surveys, while the only prospective study among these sources found only a weak, uncertain link for the place and the people. In that study (Haijen et al., 2018; about 198 self-selected adults who planned an experience on their own initiative), a good feeling about the people who would be present and about the place, rated within the day before, went with slightly lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores rated about a day after (standardized beta −0.14, p = 0.070, not statistically significant), and with slightly higher well-being two weeks later (1.2 points on the well-being scale per standard deviation of the rating, p = 0.037, one of many coefficients in a model without correction for multiple tests; not significant at four weeks, p = 0.077); a retreat or a setting designed for therapy, reported afterwards in two yes-or-no questions that the authors combined into one variable, showed no statistically significant association with any acute measure (0.02), and the authors note that the term was not defined for participants. In an international online survey of 6,877 self-selected people who had drunk ayahuasca, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety at their last ceremony went with 0.29 points less extreme fear or panic on a 0-to-10 scale (95% CI 0.15 to 0.43, editors' calculation), slightly fewer difficulties in the weeks after, and current distress lower by 0.62 points on the 40-point Kessler scale, under 2 points across the whole rating (editors' arithmetic), after adjustment for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink and for the motivation, ceremony and other support variables; the ratings were made looking back by the same people, and averaged near the top of the scale (Perkins et al., 2021). Among 613 US adults in an online panel who had used a classic psychedelic, those who blamed a lack of psychological support for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.25) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.85, 95% CI 1.27 to 6.42, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any); blaming a disagreeable physical environment went with a smaller difference in challenge (0.09) and no detectable difference in harm thoughts, and blaming the people around with no statistically significant difference in either (odds ratio for harm thoughts 0.33, 0.11 to 1.01, p = 0.051, lower if anything) (Simonsson et al., 2023). Among 163 experienced people recalling two experiences, mostly at home or at a friend's house, those whose experience was at a party, club or festival (24 first and 12 most recent experiences) had higher average challenge scores than the rest (19 against 17 and 31 against 16 per cent of the maximum), a comparison the authors did not test (Palmer and Maynard, 2022). An opinion piece by the same group as the prospective study (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) previewed, without methods, preliminary models from what appears to be an earlier cut of the same survey (266 people who completed four surveys), in which a 'therapeutic setting' (how it was recorded is not given) went with more peak or mystical-type experiences and trust in the people who would be present, rated beforehand, with less challenging ones; in the prospective study above, which appears to be the fuller report, a similar rating of the people and the place showed only a non-significant trend and a retreat or therapeutic setting no statistically significant association, so the preview is not counted as a further study and its figures are not used. No study read here put people in different places or company on purpose to compare them. The same opinion piece states that, by 2018 and apart from a dose study, retrospective analyses and one 1969 study, controlled studies isolating contextual factors had not been done, and a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023, found no trial that compared settings (Estric et al., 2025; the trials were not appraised); in those trials, 12 kept two staff in the room throughout the session and five, published in 2023, one per participant, and rooms ranged from a hospital room left unchanged (4 trials) to one disguised as a living room or decorated; the review's authors judged that the decision to disguise the room, rather than only make it more pleasant, appeared to have been taken arbitrarily, without evidence. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In surveys, people who felt safe and supported during a trip reported a little less fear and fewer difficulties, but they rated both afterwards. The only study among these that asked people beforehand found only a weak, uncertain link between feeling good about the place and the people and how the trip went, and no detectable difference for retreats or settings designed for therapy. No study we read put people in different places, or with different people, on purpose to compare them: a review of 25 clinical trials found none that compared settings, and the trials set up their rooms and staff in very different ways.
population: People who use classic psychedelics outside laboratories: adults who planned an experience on their own initiative (one prospective study), people who drink ayahuasca (one international survey), a US online panel and a self-selected survey of experienced people
exposure: The place and the people: feelings about the setting rated the day before; a retreat or therapeutic setting; support and safety at an ayahuasca ceremony rated afterwards; lack of support, a disagreeable place or disagreeable company blamed for the most challenging experience; party, club or festival settings
comparator: People who rated the setting less favourably, did not blame it, or used elsewhere, within each study
outcome: Challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire), extreme fear or panic, difficulties in the weeks after, thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others, and current distress (Kessler-10)
magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018): setting component and challenging experience beta −0.14 (p = 0.070); setting component and well-being at two weeks 1.2 points per standard deviation (p = 0.037; at four weeks p = 0.077); retreat or therapeutic setting 0.02 (p = 0.81). Perkins et al. (2021), per point of a 1-to-4 support-and-safety rating: extreme fear (0 to 10) −0.29 (95% CI −0.43 to −0.15, editors'), integration difficulties −0.13, Kessler-10 −0.62 (under 2 points across the whole rating); the paper does not say which outcomes were modelled as ordinal, so reading −0.29 as points on the fear item assumes a linear model. Simonsson et al. (2023), attributions of the most challenging experience, adjusted only for the other attributions: no support beta 0.25, harm thoughts or attempts OR 2.85 (1.27 to 6.42); disagreeable physical environment 0.09, OR 0.88 (0.33 to 2.35); disagreeable social environment not associated, OR 0.33 (0.11 to 1.01, p = 0.051). Palmer and Maynard (2022), untested: party settings 19.27 against 16.77 (first) and 31.46 against 16.16 (most recent) per cent of the maximum CEQ score.

risk_of_bias.note: Retrospective ratings or attributions made by the same people at the same sitting as the outcome, in self-selected samples, with little or no adjustment (very high risk: sc_perkins_2021, sc_simonsson_2023, sc_palmer_2022); the prospective study is at high risk (confounding, heavy attrition) and its retreat item was undefined (sc_haijen_2018).

inconsistency.note: The direction differs by aspect: support and safety went with fewer difficulties in two retrospective surveys, but blaming the people around showed no association with challenge (and, if anything, lower odds of harm thoughts) in the panel survey; in the prospective study the setting rating showed only a non-significant trend in the same direction, and a retreat or therapeutic setting no association.

indirectness.note: Worded for the people and settings studied.

imprecision.note: Large surveys; the prospective coefficient's interval includes zero, which the statement says.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, giving very low (the floor). Status mixed: four independent studies; support and safety went with fewer difficulties in two retrospective surveys (Perkins et al.; the no-support attribution in Simonsson et al.) and the untested party comparison points the same way, but blaming the people around showed no such link, and the one prospective study found only a non-significant trend for its setting rating (and a weak link with well-being two weeks later) and no association for a retreat or therapeutic setting; recall at the same sitting may explain part of the difference, but no study has shown that it does. Two further sources change neither the certainty nor the status: an opinion piece from the same group (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018), whose preliminary survey figure appears to come from an earlier cut of the prospective study's sample and gives no methods, is not counted (opinion pieces are not evidence for empirical claims, METHODS §3.2), and the associations it showed for trust and a therapeutic setting were not significant in the fuller report; a systematic review of how 25 psychiatric trials reported set and setting (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; a map of reporting, not of effects) found no trial comparing settings up to December 2023. A trial analysis in which the quality of the therapeutic alliance correlated with emotional breakthrough and mystical-type experience (Murphy et al., 2022), cited by that review, has not been read.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music played during a psychedelic session changes how it goes or what follows: no study read here compared sessions with and without music, and the one randomized comparison of two kinds of music, in 10 people, found no detectable difference, with intervals too wide to rule one out. In an open-label trial of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (Kaelen et al., 2018), 19 patients each had two psilocybin sessions lying with eye-shades in a furnished room in a clinical research facility, with two therapists and one standard playlist (one patient who strongly disliked it in the first session heard a different playlist in the second). In interviews a week after the second session, 18 of 19 described welcome influences of the music (it intensified the experience for 17, guided 15 and calmed 10) and 10 of 19 unwelcome ones (it intensified feelings they did not want, or felt uncomfortable or irritating); 9 resisted where the music was taking them and 6 felt misguided by it, mostly by music that clashed with what they were going through. Four researchers' ratings of how much each patient had liked the music, resonated with it and been open to it, made from those interviews, correlated with the fall in self-rated depression recorded at the same time point, a week after the second session (liking r = 0.60, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.83; resonance 0.59, 0.19 to 0.82; openness 0.57, 0.16 to 0.81; editors' intervals), while the patients' own rating of how intense the drug had been did not (r = 0.004, −0.45 to 0.46). The music was rated after any improvement had happened, at the same time point, so patients who felt better may have described it more warmly; the three ratings were so closely related (r 0.90 to 0.96) that they probably measure one thing, agreement between the raters averaged r = 0.6 (the authors call this good), nothing was adjusted, and the authors say that without a placebo condition causal inferences are problematic. In a US online panel of 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, 30 (4.9%) named disagreeable music among the things associated with their most challenging experience; naming it was not associated with how challenging they rated the experience (standardized beta 0.05, p = 0.19) nor, with an interval too wide to tell, with thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21, with the other listed factors entered together), and 99 (16.2%) ticked changing the music among actions that had helped during it (Simonsson et al., 2023). In the one randomized comparison of music (Strickland et al., 2021), 10 adults who smoked (8 men; mean age 51), in an open-label pilot of psilocybin to help people stop smoking, each had one session with a Western classical playlist and one with an 'overtone-based' playlist of instruments such as singing bowls, gongs and didgeridoo, in random, counterbalanced order, wearing an eye mask and headphones, with a lower dose in the first session than in the second for all but one (study conditions; the analysis adjusted for dose). Mystical-type scores (MEQ30, self-rated at the end of each session and printed on a 0-to-1 scale) averaged 0.68 with the overtone playlist and 0.52 with the classical one, a difference of 0.16 (standardized 0.57; editors' 95% CI for the difference about −0.04 to 0.36, from rounded figures) that was not statistically significant (p = 0.107); Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores were almost the same (0.33 against 0.34; standardized difference −0.11, editors' interval about −0.73 to 0.51; p = 0.74). The data therefore fit anything from slightly lower to much higher mystical-type scores with the overtone playlist, and from a moderate fall to a moderate rise in challenge. About a quarter of the classical playlist's tracks were also on the overtone playlist, about an hour of each person's own chosen music was played in every session for nine of the ten (one chose none), the overtone playlist lost three tracks after the first three people, and everyone knew which music they heard. Six of the ten then chose the overtone playlist for a third session; smoking abstinence at the end of treatment (5 of 6 who chose it against 2 of 4 who chose the classical one; editors' Fisher p = 0.50) compares people who chose differently after hearing both playlists, so it cannot show an effect of the music. In a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025), the text reports 16 trials playing a set playlist through headphones, although Table 3 describes one of those trials with stereo speakers; one alternated music and silence, two allowed no music, and none compared settings; trials treating substance use, such as the smoking pilot, were outside its scope. An older study that compared five musical conditions, no music among them, during LSD sessions for alcohol use (Gaston and Eagle, 1970) is described by Strickland et al. as finding no significant differences, in a between-subject, partly non-random design without an objective clinical outcome; it has not been read here. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study of 19 patients given psilocybin in a clinic, almost all said the music helped at times, and about half said it sometimes made things harder. Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression, but both were measured at the same time, a week later, so feeling better may have coloured how they described the music. In a trial of 10 people, each heard classical music in one psilocybin session and music of gongs and singing bowls in another, in random order; how mystical or difficult the sessions felt did not clearly differ, but the trial was too small to rule out a real difference. None of the studies we read compared sessions with and without music.
population: Patients with treatment-resistant depression in an open-label psilocybin trial (19); adults who smoked, in an open-label psilocybin smoking-cessation pilot (10, with the order of two playlists randomized); and US adults who had used classic psychedelics in an online panel (613)
exposure: Music played during psilocybin sessions: one standard playlist (with one exception), as patients described it a week later; a Western classical or an overtone-based playlist, in randomized order within each person; disagreeable music named as associated with a most challenging experience
comparator: No study had a session without music: the other playlist in the same person (randomized comparison); patients who described the music less favourably; panel respondents who did not name the music
outcome: What patients said the music did; fall in self-rated depression (QIDS) one week after; mystical-type experience (MEQ30) and challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire) self-rated after each session; smoking abstinence by chosen playlist; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others in the days or weeks after
magnitude: Kaelen et al. (2018), n = 19: welcome influences 18 of 19, unwelcome 10 of 19; QIDS fall with music liking r = 0.60 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.83, editors'), resonance 0.59, openness 0.57; drug intensity r = 0.004 (−0.45 to 0.46). Simonsson et al. (2023): disagreeable music named by 30 of 613, not associated with challenge (beta 0.05, p = 0.19) or, imprecisely, with later thoughts or attempts of harm (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21); changing the music ticked as helpful by 99 of 613. Strickland et al. (2021), n = 10, randomized sessions 1 and 2: MEQ30 0.68 (SD 0.20) overtone against 0.52 (SD 0.21) Western classical, dz 0.57, p = 0.107 (dose-adjusted b = 0.14, p = 0.108); editors' 95% CI for the difference about −0.04 to 0.36 (dz about −0.12 to 1.23); CEQ 0.33 (SD 0.20) against 0.34 (SD 0.22), dz −0.11, p = 0.74 (editors' dz interval about −0.73 to 0.51). Abstinence by chosen playlist, not randomized: 5 of 6 (overtone) against 2 of 4 (classical) at the end of treatment and 4 of 6 against 2 of 4 at long-term follow-up (editors' Fisher p = 0.50 and 1.0).

risk_of_bias.note: The randomized genre comparison has some concerns (card sc_strickland_2021): open label, self-ratings by participants who knew which music they heard, the overtone playlist changed after three participants, no registered analysis plan, and period effects untested. The music-experience ratings in the depression trial come from interviews at the same time point as the outcome, with no adjustment and no music-free condition (card sc_kaelen_2018, overall very high), and the panel survey's attributions are retrospective (sc_simonsson_2023); both are worded only as associations.

inconsistency.note: The sources answer different questions (two playlists compared, how patients experienced one playlist, music named in a survey).

indirectness.note: The randomized comparison tested two genres, not music against silence, with about a quarter of the classical tracks shared and personal music in each session for nine of ten participants (one chose none), in 10 people in a smoking-cessation pilot; the other sources are a hospital trial of patients with depression and a US panel.

imprecision.note: 10 people in the randomized comparison, with intervals from slightly lower to much higher mystical-type scores and from a moderate fall to a moderate rise in challenge; 19 patients for the main correlation (interval 0.20 to 0.83); the panel's harm estimate for music rests on 30 people (interval 0.87 to 8.21).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; no registered analysis plan is reported for the genre comparison.

grade.reasoning: Rated from the one randomized comparison, the best evidence on whether the music itself changes a session: randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias, one for indirectness and two for imprecision, giving very low (the floor). The correlational evidence on how patients experienced the music (Kaelen et al., 2018) is very low on its own, as before (low, minus two for risk of bias and one for imprecision). Worded as insufficient evidence because neither an effect of the music nor its absence can be shown with precision. Status single study: each question rests on one small study (two genres compared in 10 people; the music experience and the fall in depression in 19 patients); the panel survey adds only null associations, one very imprecise, for music named as associated with a difficult experience. A systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low) found none that compared settings, music included; trials treating substance use were outside its scope. The published correction to Strickland et al. (2021; doi 10.1021/acsptsci.1c00119), read on 12 November 2026, changes only the acknowledgments, so no figure here is affected. The only comparison with a no-music condition in psychedelic sessions that these sources mention, a 1970 quasi-randomized study of LSD sessions (Gaston and Eagle), is known only from Strickland et al.'s description and has not been read. A 2025 opinion article argues against music in therapy settings and notes that no controlled study compares music with silence; it has no card.

statement: In an online panel of US adults matched to the population on sex, age and ethnicity only (Prolific, October 2021; Simonsson et al., 2023), 613 of 2,822 respondents (21.7%) had ever used a classic psychedelic (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, mescaline, peyote or San Pedro). Asked once, looking back over their whole life, 362 of the 613 (59.1%) said they had never had a challenging, difficult or distressing experience with them, 143 (23.3%) rarely, 80 (13.1%) occasionally and 28 (4.6%) regularly or frequently: 41 in 100 at least once (editors' calculation). 28 (4.6%) said their ability to function had been severely impaired, and 55 (9.0%; printed 8.9%) that impairment had lasted more than a day, 21 of them (3.4%) more than a month (editors' sum), but the two impairment questions gave counts that do not agree (176 reported some impairment, 262 gave its length). All 613, including the 362 who said they had never had one, were asked about their most challenging experience; in the days or weeks after it, 41 (6.7%) reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others, including 9 (1.5%) attempts to harm themselves, and 16 (2.6%) sought medical, psychiatric or psychological help. 350 (57.1%) reported at least one symptom lasting at least a few days that they put down to psychedelics, most often feeling anxious (36.1%) or difficulty sleeping (27.9%), but these questions, borrowed from meditation research, were not asked of people who had not used psychedelics or about times without them, so how many such symptoms would have happened anyway is unknown; 482 (78.6%) agreed, at least slightly, that they were glad to have used psychedelics. Challenging experiences were linked most often to LSD (by 31.5% of those who had used it, against 19.7% for psilocybin, ayahuasca or DMT and 14.7% for mescaline, peyote or San Pedro), but how often each drug had been used was not asked. The 8 people taking lithium and the 16 taking another mood stabilizer at the time of their most challenging experience had higher odds of later harm thoughts or attempts (odds ratios 22.34, 95% CI 1.78 to 279.65, and 5.84, 1.40 to 24.34, adjusted only for the other medicines), estimates too imprecise, and too open to confounding by the conditions these medicines treat, to give a risk. In a self-selected online sample of people who had used psychedelics, 555 of 869 (64 in 100) said the experience they described had included a period of distress, difficulty or discomfort (Wood et al., 2024), a reminder that such figures depend on who is asked and how. In a prospective study that measured well-being before and after a planned psychedelic experience (Haijen et al., 2018), 85 of the 279 people who answered both surveys (30 in 100, editors' calculation) scored lower two weeks later, counting any fall however small, and they had not rated the experience as more challenging than the others (the paper gives no statistics for this comparison); many who started did not answer the later surveys, and with no comparison group the fall cannot be put down to the drug. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one US online survey, 59 in 100 people who had ever used a psychedelic said they had never had a difficult experience, and 41 in 100 had had at least one. About 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life, 7 in 100 thought about or tried hurting themselves or others in the days or weeks after, and 3 in 100 got help. Many said worry or poor sleep lasted days, but nobody who had not used psychedelics was asked the same questions, so it is not known how many of these problems would have happened anyway.
population: Adults in the United States who had ever used a classic psychedelic, in an opt-in online panel matched on sex, age and ethnicity (613 of 2,822), with a self-selected online sample and one prospective cohort for comparison
exposure: Lifetime use of classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, mescaline, peyote, San Pedro)
comparator: None for the frequencies (no group without psychedelic use answered the same questions)
outcome: Challenging, difficult or distressing experiences; impaired functioning and its length; symptoms lasting days that respondents attributed to psychedelics; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others; help-seeking
magnitude: Simonsson et al. (2023), of 613: never had a challenging experience 362 (59.1%); at least once 251 (40.9%, editors'); severe impairment 28 (4.6%); impairment over a day 55 (9.0%), over a month 21 (3.4%, editors'); harm thoughts or attempts 41 (6.7%), self-harm attempts 9 (1.5%); sought help 16 (2.6%); lasting symptoms attributed to psychedelics 350 (57.1%, no comparison group); glad 482 (78.6%, slightly to strongly agree). Lithium (8 people) OR 22.34 (1.78 to 279.65), other mood stabilizers (16) 5.84 (1.40 to 24.34), adjusted only for the other medicines. Wood et al. (2024): 555 of 869 (63.9%) recalled distress in the experience they described. Haijen et al. (2018): well-being lower at two weeks (any fall) in 85 of the 279 with both measurements (30.5%).

statement: In people who had used magic mushrooms (mushrooms containing psilocybin) in the past 12 months and took part in the Global Drug Survey 2017, an anonymous online survey of drug use open from November 2016 to January 2017 in 10 languages, which people chose to join through social networks, media partners and harm-reduction organisations and were not paid for (12,534 respondents reported past-year use: 62.9% were under 25, 78.7% men, and most lived in Germany, the United States, Canada, Denmark or the United Kingdom), 19 of the 9,233 who answered the question (0.2%; about 2 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency medical treatment after using magic mushrooms in that year (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022). The denominator is the people who answered that question (74% of those reporting past-year use, editors' calculation), not everyone who reported past-year use, although the abstract describes the 9,233 as the past-year group; among the 1,895 who completed the whole survey, 1,857 answered and 6 (0.3%) said yes, which the authors read as showing that most missing answers came from people who left the survey early. Emergency treatment was not defined, answers were not checked against any record, and the number of incidents per person was not asked; dividing the 19 people by an estimated 34,347 days of use (a mean of 3.72 days a year), the authors put the figure at about 1 in 1,800 past-year intakes (0.06%). In the companion analysis of the same survey, 102 of 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year and answered (1.0%; about 10 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency treatment after LSD, which the authors describe as about five times the mushroom share (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022); per day of use, the LSD figure is about 3.4 times the mushroom figure (editors' calculation). Of the 19, 8 (42%) said they had been admitted to hospital, which the survey did not define (as the LSD paper states). They ticked a median of 5 symptoms from a list of 21: anxiety or panic 68%, paranoia 68%, seeing or hearing things 42%, passing out 37%, difficulty breathing 32% and seizures 26% (13, 13, 8, 7, 6 and 5 of the 19 by the editors' arithmetic, matching the bars of a figure that prints no values; in the same figure about 1 of the 19 ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm); the authors note that passing out may in some cases have been brief memory loss or falling asleep, and that they cannot confirm that the seizures were epileptic rather than triggered by psychological factors. Of the 18 who said how long it took to feel back to normal, 17 did so within 24 hours (12 within 6 hours) and 1 within 5 to 7 days; the authors add that 'back to normal' may for some have meant only that the acute effects had resolved. In the session that led to emergency treatment, 8 of the 19 had taken nothing else and 11 (editors' subtraction) had also taken another substance, most often cannabis (7) or alcohol (6); how often people combined substances in sessions that did not end in emergency treatment was not asked. Choosing up to three of six reasons, with no 'other' option, they named their mood or mindset (9), mixing substances (7), the place or setting (7) or taking too much (5), or did not know (4); 1 thought the drug had not been magic mushrooms. The people who sought treatment were younger (median age 19 against 23; p = 0.002); with 19 events, no difference was detected by sex, lifetime mental health diagnosis, first use in the past year, usual quantity or frequency of use. Afterwards, 58% said they had cut down their use and 37% that it had not changed. The authors write that the results 'confirm psilocybin mushrooms are a relatively safe drug' and that harm-reduction information probably does much to prevent adverse effects; the survey cannot count deaths, lasting harm or people who could not or did not answer, and harm-reduction information was not studied. The survey's founder and owner is an author; King's College London receives funding from COMPASS Pathways for psilocybin trials led by two of the authors, one of whom (Rucker) has been paid as a consultant by Clerkenwell Health and Beckley PsyTech, and the other (Young) has had honoraria and consulting fees from several drug companies and co-edits the publishing journal; the funding statement names UK National Institute for Health Research support for those two authors and no funder for the survey. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a big online drug survey in 2016 and 2017, 19 of the 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year and answered the question (about 2 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency treatment afterwards; after LSD, in the same survey, it was about 1 in 100, about five times as many. Of the 19, most had panic, anxiety or paranoia, 8 said they were admitted to hospital, and 17 of the 18 who answered felt back to normal within a day. Those who sought treatment were younger, typically 19 against 23. People chose to take part, nobody checked their answers or what they had taken, and people who could not answer were not counted.
population: Respondents to the Global Drug Survey 2017 (anonymous, online, self-nominated; November 2016 to January 2017; 10 languages) who reported magic mushroom use in the past 12 months (12,534; 62.9% under 25, 78.7% men, most living in Germany, the United States, Canada, Denmark or the United Kingdom), of whom 9,233 answered the emergency-treatment question
exposure: Use of magic mushrooms (psilocybin-containing mushrooms) in the past 12 months, self-reported; species, potency and content unknown; other substances in the incident session as reported
comparator: None outside the sample: within it, respondents who answered and did not report seeking emergency treatment (for age, sex, mental health diagnosis, first use, usual quantity and frequency of use); in the companion analysis of the same survey, respondents who had used LSD
outcome: Self-reported seeking of emergency medical treatment (not defined) after magic mushroom use in the past 12 months; for those who said yes, symptoms ticked from a list of 21, self-reported hospital admission (not defined), time to feel back to normal, other substances in that session, perceived reasons and change in use
magnitude: Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al. (2022): 19 of 9,233 who answered (0.2%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 0.13% to 0.32%); completers 6 of 1,857 (0.3%); per day of use 0.00055 (0.06%, about 1 in 1,800; 19 divided by an estimated 34,347 days). Of the 19: hospital admission 8 (42%; printed 95% CI 20–64%; editors' Wilson 23% to 64%); anxiety or panic 68%, paranoia 68%, seeing or hearing things 42%, passing out 37%, difficulty breathing 32%, seizures 26%; back to normal within 24 hours 17 of 18, within 5 to 7 days 18 of 18; nothing else taken 8, cannabis 7, alcohol 6; reasons mood or mindset 9, mixing 7, setting 7, too much 5, don't know 4, not magic mushrooms 1; median age 19 against 23 (p = 0.002). Companion LSD analysis (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022): 102 of 10,293 (1.0%); editors' calculation: about 4.8 times the mushroom share per person and about 3.4 times per day of use.

evidence.extracted: Secondary analysis of the Global Drug Survey (GDS) 2017, an anonymous, encrypted online drug survey run every year; people nominate themselves after seeing it promoted on social networks by media partners and harm-reduction organisations. This round was open from November 2016 to January 2017, in 10 languages, without payment. People who reported magic mushroom use in the past 12 months were asked on how many days they had used them in that period, whether that period included their first use, how many mushrooms they usually take on days they use them, and whether they had sought emergency medical treatment (EMT) after magic mushrooms in the past year; how many such incidents each person had was not recorded. People who said yes ticked their symptoms from a list of 21 drawn from the literature and answered questions on the mushrooms and any other substances taken in that session, how long the symptoms lasted, whether hospital care had been needed, up to three of six possible reasons, and any change in their later use. The abstract states the aim as the 12-month prevalence of such incidents and reports 19 (0.2%) of 9233, presented there as the past-year group.

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement (card sc_kopra_2022, JBI prevalence checklist, high): one undefined, unvalidated yes-or-no item covering 12 months, with respondents themselves linking the incident to magic mushrooms; symptoms, hospital admission and recovery are self-reported and unverified, with no records or toxicology; 26% of those reporting past-year use did not answer the item (the completer check, 6 of 1,857, points to drop-out rather than selective skipping, but the authors say skipping could bias the rate either way); incidents per person were not recorded.

inconsistency.note: One survey; the LSD figure comes from a companion analysis of the same survey about another drug and is reported as a comparison within that survey, not as a second estimate.

indirectness.note: Coverage: respondents chose to join a survey promoted through social networks, media partners and harm-reduction organisations, with no sampling frame; mostly young men living in Europe or North America, in 2016–17; people who died, were badly harmed or could not answer online are outside the design. The figure describes these respondents, not people who use magic mushrooms in general, and it is not a risk per occasion.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: the headline share is precise for the sample (19 of 9,233; editors' Wilson 95% interval 0.13% to 0.32%). Every statement about the incidents rests on 19 people and is given as counts with their denominators; the certainty is already at the floor.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled (METHODS §6.3): starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low, the floor; never upgraded. 'Describes' because it reports how many respondents said they had sought emergency treatment, not a risk for people who use magic mushrooms and not a cause of the symptoms. The question is worded with 'seek', not 'need', because the survey asked whether people had sought emergency treatment, not whether they needed it. Status single study: one survey wave; the LSD figure comes from a companion analysis of the same survey by the same team and is a comparison within that survey, not a replication. The per-day figure is the authors' calculation and counts each person once. The authors' conclusions that the results confirm relative safety and that harm-reduction information plays a key role are not adopted: the survey could not count deaths or people who did not answer, and harm-reduction information was not studied. Numbers of mushrooms are left out, and 'taking too much' appears only as a reason respondents chose.

statement: In adults with moderate to severe major depression in two randomized trials, all off antidepressants for at least 2 weeks before dosing, one dose of psilocybin given by clinicians in the trial with psychological support (trial conditions: 25 mg, with preparation sessions beforehand, a supervised session of 6 to 10 hours with two therapists or facilitators, and integration sessions afterwards) compared with the same support and a 1-mg dose of psilocybin or a capsule of niacin is associated with larger falls in clinician-rated depression scores 3 and 6 weeks later. In 233 adults with treatment-resistant depression (no response to two to four adequate treatments in the current episode) at 22 sites in Europe and North America, 2019 to 2021, the MADRS (0 to 60) fell by 12.0 points after 25 mg, 7.9 after 10 mg and 5.4 after 1 mg by week 3, the primary end point: a difference of −6.6 points for 25 mg against 1 mg (95% CI −10.2 to −2.9), while 10 mg did not differ from 1 mg (−2.5, −6.2 to 1.2; P = 0.18) (Goodwin et al., 2022). Because the 10-mg comparison failed, the prespecified testing order stopped, so every secondary result, including those for 25 mg, counts formally as not significant: at week 3, 29 of 79 given 25 mg (37 in 100) and 14 of 79 given 1 mg (18 in 100) had responded (a fall of half or more), and 23 of 79 (29 in 100) and 6 of 79 (8 in 100) were in remission; a response kept from week 3 through week 12 was seen in 16 of 79 (20 in 100) against 8 of 79 (10 in 100) (odds ratio 2.2, 0.9 to 5.4). Between weeks 3 and 12, 26 of the 79 given 25 mg (33 in 100) started another treatment for depression, as did 16 of 79 given 1 mg. Serious adverse events of suicidal ideation or self-injury from day 2 to week 3 occurred in 4 of 79 given 25 mg, 3 of 75 given 10 mg (besides 1 hospitalization for severe depression) and none of 79 given 1 mg; after week 3, suicidal behaviour in 3 given 25 mg (all with earlier suicidal behaviour or self-injury and no response at week 3), self-injury or suicidal ideation in 2 given 10 mg and self-injury in 1 given 1 mg (counts by period; the number of distinct people over the 12 weeks is not given). The trial was designed and funded by COMPASS Pathfinder, the company whose proprietary psilocybin formulation was tested, which also did the interpretation and post hoc analyses; 8 of the 74 authors are listed with the company, and the authors' disclosure forms are not printed in the article. In 104 adults with major depression (a current episode of at least 60 days; 13 of 104 met the trial's definition of treatment resistance) at 11 US sites, 2019 to 2022, scores fell by 19.1 points after psilocybin and 6.8 after niacin, a vitamin that causes flushing, given as an active placebo in identical capsules, by day 43, the primary end point: a difference of −12.3 points (95% CI −17.5 to −7.2), with −12.0 by day 8 and no difference at day 2 (−0.1) (Raison et al., 2023; version corrected on 26 January 2024). Among those assessed at every visit, 20 of 48 assigned to psilocybin (42 in 100) and 5 of 44 assigned to niacin (11 in 100) kept a fall of half or more from day 8 to day 43, which the authors call a sustained response; sustained remission did not differ significantly (12 of 48 against 4 of 44; P = .05). By 6 weeks, 1 of 51 assigned to psilocybin and 9 of 53 assigned to niacin had withdrawn or been lost to follow-up. The authors call the reduction clinically significant, but no threshold for a meaningful difference was set in advance (they argue it afterwards from published values, using the point estimate; the interval reaches 7.2 points, below the 9 points they cite), 'sustained' means through day 43, and they state that the trial cannot show whether the effect would have faded later. No serious adverse events followed dosing and no suicidal or self-injurious behaviour was recorded; from the dosing day through day 9, adverse events judged related to the drug affected 41 of 50 given psilocybin (82 in 100) and 24 of 54 given niacin (44 in 100), and severe related events 4 of 50 and none. Some relative incidences and intervals printed for these adverse events do not fit their counts, so the counts are used (Raison et al., 2023). That trial was sponsored and funded by the Usona Institute, a non-profit medical research organization that supplied the psilocybin, designed the trial, interpreted the data and wrote the manuscript; 8 of the 35 authors are listed at the institute, and many authors report fees, grants or shares from companies developing psychedelic and other medicines. Neither trial checked whether participants could tell which they had received; both sets of authors say the acute effects of psilocybin probably weakened the blinding, and the Raison authors say this may have contributed to the effect and to the higher dropout with niacin. A two-page viewpoint on the Goodwin trial, with no data of its own, by an author of the Raison trial report who was not part of the Goodwin team (Gukasyan, 2023), singles out the missing blinding check as perhaps that trial's most serious flaw and argues that the suicidal behaviour of three participants given 25 mg, all with no response at week 3 and earlier suicide attempts or self-injury, should be taken seriously; events coded as suicidal behaviour were indeed all in the 25-mg group, but, as the trial's abstract states, suicidal ideation, behaviour or self-injury occurred in every dose group, serious events included (counted above). The MADRS was rated by remote raters who did not know the group, from participants' own answers. Neither trial compared psilocybin with an established treatment or with an inert placebo; both excluded people judged to be at current risk of suicide and people with psychotic depression (Raison: any personal or first-degree family history of psychosis or mania), and most participants were White. These results describe psilocybin given in a medical trial with screening and psychological support, not use outside such settings. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In two trials, adults with depression who had stopped their antidepressants were picked at random for one dose of psilocybin, given in a clinic with two therapists or guides, with preparation beforehand and talks afterwards, or for the same care with a tiny dose of psilocybin or with a vitamin pill (niacin) that makes the skin flush. In 233 adults whose depression had not eased with two to four treatments, depression scores had fallen more after the full dose than after the tiny dose at 3 weeks, by 6.6 points on a 60-point scale; a medium dose did no better than the tiny one. At 3 weeks, 37 in 100 on the full dose and 18 in 100 on the tiny dose had their scores at least halved, but under the trial's own rules this could not count as proven, and by 12 weeks the gap (20 in 100 against 10 in 100 still much better) could be chance; by then a third of the full-dose group had started another treatment. Serious events of suicidal thoughts or self-harm happened on the full and medium doses, and once on the tiny dose. In 104 US adults, only about 1 in 8 of whom had depression that two or more medicines had failed to ease, scores fell 12.3 points more with psilocybin than with the vitamin pill over 6 weeks, and 42 in 100 against 11 in 100 stayed much better throughout; 1 person in the psilocybin group and 9 in the vitamin-pill group dropped out. Nobody had a serious side effect after the dose, but headache and nausea were common. Neither trial checked whether people could tell what they had taken, and both sets of authors say the strong effects of psilocybin probably gave it away. A researcher who also worked on the US trial later criticised the bigger trial for not checking this, and urged that the suicidal behaviour of three people on the full dose be taken seriously. The organizations that supplied the psilocybin paid for both trials and interpreted the results.
population: Adults with moderate to severe major depression in two randomized trials: 233 outpatients with treatment-resistant depression (no response to two to four adequate treatments in the current episode; episodes without psychotic features; mean age 39.8; 121 women; 215 White; 14 had used psilocybin before; mean baseline MADRS 32.5) at 22 sites in 10 countries in Europe and North America, March 2019 to September 2021 (Goodwin et al., 2022); and 104 medically healthy adults aged 21 to 65 with major depressive disorder (current episode of at least 60 days; central-rater MADRS of 28 or more at screening; 13 meeting the trial's definition of treatment resistance; median one earlier medicine in the current episode; mean age 41.1; 52 women; 89% White; mean baseline MADRS 35.5 and 35.0) at 11 US sites, December 2019 to June 2022 (Raison et al., 2023). All were off antidepressants for at least 2 weeks before dosing. Goodwin excluded people judged to be at clinically significant risk of suicide; Raison excluded active suicidal ideation with intent or plan, suicidal behaviour in the past 12 months, a personal or first-degree family history of psychosis or mania, moderate or severe alcohol or drug use disorder, and any psychedelic use in the past 5 years or more than 10 lifetime uses.
exposure: One dose of psilocybin given by clinicians in the trial with psychological support (trial conditions: 25 mg of the proprietary synthetic formulation COMP360 in Goodwin et al., where 10 mg was also tested; 25 mg of synthetic psilocybin by mouth in Raison et al.), after preparation sessions (at least three therapist meetings; 6 to 8 hours with two facilitators), in a supervised session of 6 to 8 hours with two therapists (Goodwin) or 7 to 10 hours with two facilitators (Raison), followed by integration sessions
comparator: The same preparation, session and integration with a 1-mg dose of the same psilocybin formulation (Goodwin et al., 2022) or with 100 mg of niacin, a vitamin that causes flushing, given as an active placebo in identical-looking capsules (Raison et al., 2023); no inert placebo and no established treatment
outcome: Clinician-rated depression on the MADRS (0 to 60), rated by telephone by remote raters who did not know the group: change from baseline to week 3 (Goodwin, primary) and to day 43 (Raison, primary); response, remission and sustained response; dropout and starting other treatment; adverse events, including serious events of suicidal ideation, self-injury or suicidal behaviour
magnitude: Goodwin et al. (2022), modified intention-to-treat (79, 75, 79): MADRS least-squares mean change to week 3 −12.0 (95% CI −14.6 to −9.3) with 25 mg, −7.9 (−10.6 to −5.2) with 10 mg, −5.4 (−8.1 to −2.7) with 1 mg; difference 25 mg against 1 mg −6.6 (−10.2 to −2.9), P<0.001; 10 mg against 1 mg −2.5 (−6.2 to 1.2), P = 0.18. Secondary, formally not significant because hierarchical testing stopped: response at week 3 29/79 (37%) against 14/79 (18%), odds ratio 2.9 (1.2 to 6.6); remission 23/79 (29%) against 6/79 (8%), 4.8 (1.8 to 12.8); sustained response to week 12 16/79 (20%) against 8/79 (10%), 2.2 (0.9 to 5.4). Editors' calculation (Wald): response difference 19.0 percentage points (5.4 to 32.5); remission 21.5 (9.9 to 33.1); sustained response 10.1 (−1.0 to 21.2); standardized difference for the primary contrast about 0.55 (SD about 11.9, back-calculated from the SE of the difference, 1.9). New depression treatment from week 3 to week 12: 26/79 (33%), 18/75 (24%), 16/79 (20%); before week 3: 4/79, 9/75, 14/79. Serious adverse events of suicidal ideation, self-injury or suicidal behaviour: day 2 to week 3, 4/79, 3/75, 0/79; after week 3, 3/79, 2/75, 1/79 (by period). Raison et al. (2023), intention to treat (51, 53): MADRS change to day 43 −19.1 (−22.7 to −15.5) against −6.8 (−10.5 to −3.1), difference −12.3 (−17.5 to −7.2), P<.001; day 8 −12.0 (−16.6 to −7.4), P<.001; day 2 −0.1 (−2.1 to 1.9). Sustained response 20/48 (41.7%) against 5/44 (11.4%), difference 30.3 percentage points (13.5 to 47.1), odds ratio 5.60 (1.87 to 16.74), P = .002; sustained remission 12/48 (25.0%) against 4/44 (9.1%), odds ratio 3.37 (0.99 to 11.47), P = .05. Withdrawn or lost by week 6: 1/51 against 9/53. Related adverse events from dosing to day 9: 41/50 (82%) against 24/54 (44%); severe related 4/50 against 0/54; no serious adverse events after dosing. Editors' calculation: standardized difference at day 43 about 1.0 (SD about 12.7, back-calculated from the interval with 50 and 44 assessed).

evidence.locator: Abstract (Methods, Results, Conclusions) (p. 1637); Methods › Trial Oversight, 1st paragraph, and Participants, 1st paragraph (p. 1638); Methods › Trial Design and Procedures, 1st to 3rd paragraphs, and Efficacy End Points, 1st paragraph (p. 1639)
evidence.extracted: Phase 2, double-blind, dose-finding, parallel-group randomized trial at 22 sites in 10 countries in Europe (Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, United Kingdom) and North America (Canada, United States), 1 March 2019 to 27 September 2021. Outpatients aged 18 or older with a DSM-5 major depressive episode without psychotic features whose current episode had not responded to two to four adequate treatments (adequate dose and at least 8 weeks, by the MGH ATRQ), recruited through referrals from primary care and specialist psychiatry services, online advertisements and word of mouth. During a 3-to-6-week run-in, antidepressants and other prohibited medicines acting on the central nervous system were tapered and stopped at least 2 weeks before baseline, and each participant met a therapist at least three times. Randomized 1:1:1 at a central location, stratified by country and previous psilocybin experience, to a single dose of COMP360, the sponsor's proprietary synthetic psilocybin formulation, of 25 mg, 10 mg or 1 mg (the control), with psychological support: an administration session of 6 to 8 hours with the lead therapist and an assisting therapist, in rooms designed to be calm and non-clinical, with a music playlist and eyeshades; integration sessions on day 2 and at week 1; follow-up for 12 weeks. Participants were asked to stay off antidepressants for the first 3 weeks, though a physician investigator could start them at any time if clinically necessary. Therapists did not know the assignments and collected no efficacy data; the MADRS was rated by telephone by trained remote raters of an independent contract research organization who did not know the trial details or assignments. The sponsor, COMPASS Pathfinder, designed and funded the trial; a contract research organization paid by the sponsor supervised it and did the statistical analysis, which the sponsor reviewed; the sponsor did the interpretation and post hoc analyses and paid for professional writing assistance with the first draft; confidentiality agreements were in place between the investigators and the sponsor.

evidence.locator: Methods › Efficacy End Points, 1st paragraph (p. 1639, continued on p. 1640); Methods › Safety End Points, and Statistical Analysis, 1st to 5th paragraphs (p. 1640)
evidence.extracted: Primary end point: change in MADRS total score (0 to 60) from baseline (the day before dosing) to week 3, comparing 25 mg and 10 mg each with 1 mg; MADRS also on day 2 and at weeks 1, 6, 9 and 12. Three key secondary end points: response (a fall of at least 50% from baseline to week 3), remission (MADRS of 10 or less at week 3) and sustained response (a week-3 response maintained through week 12). Suicidal ideation with intent, or endorsement of any item of the suicidal-behaviour section of the Columbia scale, including non-suicidal self-injurious behaviour, was reported as a serious adverse event. Planned sample 216 (72 per group) for 90% power at two-sided 0.05 to detect a 6-point difference, assuming a common standard deviation of 11.0; efficacy analysed in the modified intention-to-treat set. For participants who started a new antidepressant treatment, later MADRS scores were imputed with a missing-not-at-random method that progressively worsened them, and the same method was applied after withdrawal for lack of efficacy or adverse events; for response, remission and sustained response such participants counted as not responding. A hierarchical test procedure covered the primary and three key secondary end points, examining 25 mg and then 10 mg for each end point before moving to the next, at two-sided 0.05.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 843); Methods › Study Design Overview and Oversight, Participants, and Study Procedures, 1st paragraph (p. 844, continued on p. 845); Study Procedures, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 845)
evidence.extracted: Phase 2, randomized, two-group trial at 11 US sites, December 2019 to June 2022 (the PDF is the version corrected on 26 January 2024). Recruitment through a study website, clinical programmes at the sites, advertisements, and clinician and patient-advocate listservs. Medically healthy adults aged 21 to 65 with DSM-5 major depressive disorder, a current episode of at least 60 days and a central-rater MADRS of 28 or more at screening, with no more than 30% improvement during a 7-to-35-day period allowing a taper of psychiatric medicines (no antidepressants for at least 2 weeks or 5 half-lives, whichever was longer). Excluded: personal or first-degree family history of psychosis or mania; moderate or severe alcohol or drug use disorder; inability or unwillingness to stop prohibited psychotropic medicines; any psychedelic use in the past 5 years or more than 10 lifetime uses; active suicidal ideation with intent or plan; suicidal behaviour in the past 12 months; previous deep brain or vagus nerve stimulation, as a proxy for severe treatment resistance. Randomized 1:1 on the dosing day (permuted blocks of 2, 4 and 6, stratified by site, administered centrally through the contract research organization's data system) to one oral dose of 25 mg synthetic psilocybin or 100 mg niacin in identical-looking capsules; niacin was used as an active placebo that produces flushing, thought to aid blinding. Both groups had the same protocol: 6 to 8 hours of preparation with two facilitators, a 7-to-10-hour dosing session supervised by them, with eyeshades and a playlist on headphones encouraged, and 4 hours of integration; lead facilitators were doctoral-level psychologists or physicians experienced in treating depression. Participants, sponsor and site staff did not know the assignments until data lock.

evidence.locator: Methods › Efficacy Assessments, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, and Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 845); Statistical Analysis, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 846)
evidence.extracted: Primary outcome: between-group difference in mean change in central-rater MADRS (0 to 60) from baseline to day 43; key secondary: the same at day 8; other secondary: the Sheehan Disability Scale at day 43, and sustained response (a fall of at least 50% from baseline at each of days 8, 15, 29 and 43) and sustained remission (MADRS of 10 or less at each of those visits), both defined a priori. A minimal clinically important difference for the MADRS was not prespecified; the authors cite literature values of 2 to 9 points for a placebo-adjusted change and of 6 (meaningful) and 12 (substantial) points for change from baseline. All MADRS ratings were done by telephone by trained remote central raters who did not know the assignment, the visit or the protocol, to reduce functional unblinding of raters. The FDA first recommended day 8 as the primary end point, and the power calculation assumed falls of 18 (day 8) and 17 (day 43) points with psilocybin and 10 with niacin, SD 10, giving 92% power for day 43 and 98% for day 8 with 100 participants; after the FDA recommended day 43, the primary end point was changed and the sample size raised from 80 to 100. Mixed model for repeated measures adjusted for baseline score, site, sex and treatment-resistant depression, without imputation; sequential testing in the order MADRS day 43, MADRS day 8, SDS day 43, sustained response, sustained remission, halted at the first P of .05 or more.

evidence.extracted: Safety population: 50 given psilocybin and 54 given niacin. At least one adverse event through day 43: 44 (88%) and 33 (61%). Three serious adverse events occurred between enrollment and randomization (nephrolithiasis, obstructive incisional hernia, appendicitis; Table 3: 1 and 2 participants) and none after dosing. From dosing (day 1) through day 9: adverse events judged related to the study drug 41 of 50 (82%) and 24 of 54 (44%); severe related events 4 of 50 (8%; migraine, headache, illusion, and panic attack with paranoia, one participant each) and none with niacin; moderate related events 11 (22%) and 2 (4%); headache 33 (66%) and 13 (24%); nausea 24 (48%) and 3 (6%); visual perceptual effects (assessed after the acute drug effects had resolved) on the dosing day 22 (44%) and 3 (6%), and after the dosing day 3 (6%) given psilocybin, all resolved by the end of the study. Day 10 to day 43: related events 2 of 50 (4%) and 1 of 53 (2%). evidence.locator: Abstract, Conclusions and Relevance (p. 843); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 848); Discussion, 3rd paragraph, and Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 849); Limitations, 3rd to 5th paragraphs (p. 850)
evidence.extracted: The abstract concludes that psilocybin was associated with a clinically significant sustained reduction in depressive symptoms and functional disability, without serious adverse events. The Discussion acknowledges that no minimal clinically important difference was specified a priori and argues clinical significance afterwards: the 12.3-point difference exceeds an upper active-placebo difference of 9 points in the literature, and the 19.1-point fall with psilocybin exceeds a 12-point threshold for substantial improvement in treatment-resistant depression. 'Sustained' refers to the 6-week follow-up: the authors state that the trial does not allow inferences on whether the effect would have diminished over later weeks or been maintained, that the earlier treatment-resistant trial (Goodwin et al.) had a 12-week follow-up during which the effect waned, and that whether their own result reflects the low rate of treatment resistance (13%) is unknown. Limitations stated: the success of blinding was not assessed, and the acute psychoactive effects of psilocybin probably produced some functional unblinding that may have contributed to the effect seen with psilocybin and to the higher dropout with niacin; the placebo response, smaller than is typical with daily placebo pills, may have inflated the effect compared with trials of standard antidepressants; fidelity to the support protocol was not assessed; the sample was predominantly White, non-Hispanic and of higher socioeconomic status. The authors compare their 8% rate of severe adverse events with a 10% rate they attribute to Goodwin et al., and note that, unlike that trial, no clinically confirmed active suicidal ideation or suicidal behaviour occurred.

evidence.extracted: Two-page viewpoint by a single author at the Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, not one of the trial's authors, on Goodwin et al. (2022), with no data of its own and ten references chosen by the author. Standfirst: the results suggest modest efficacy but raise concerns about the potential for serious adverse effects. 3rd paragraph: calls blinding perhaps the most glaring criticism, because the trial collected no data on blinding integrity although this would have been easy; cites a psilocybin trial in alcohol use disorder in which 94% of participants and 92% of staff identified the treatment correctly after the first dose, and a notice from the US National Institute of Mental Health, issued less than two weeks after the trial's publication, giving low funding priority to psychedelic trials without rigorous assessment of blinding integrity. 4th paragraph: calls the rate of adverse events relatively high, without figures; three participants had suicidal behaviour about one to two months after treatment, all non-responders at week 3 with previous suicide attempts or non-suicidal self-injury, and all suicidal behaviour in the trial occurred in the 25-mg arm, which the author says should be taken seriously. 5th paragraph: proposes, as possibilities for study, a demoralization reaction in patients who believe they received a much-publicized treatment and do not improve, the type, timing and frequency of aftercare, and challenging psychedelic experiences. The author's support came from private donors and a foundation; she declares that she is a co-investigator on a study of psilocybin for major depressive disorder funded by the Usona Institute. Editors' checks: she is listed among the authors of Raison et al. (2023, pp. 843, 851) and reports grants from the Usona Institute during that study (p. 852). Against the trial (Goodwin et al., 2022, pp. 1637, 1644–1645): events coded as suicidal behaviour (3 participants, after week 3) were all in the 25-mg group, but the trial's abstract states that suicidal ideation or behaviour or self-injury occurred in all dose groups, and its Results report serious suicidal ideation or self-injury with 25 mg and 10 mg from day 2 to week 3 and intentional self-injury in 1 participant given 1 mg after week 3; worsening of suicidal state from baseline to week 3 was most frequent with 10 mg (13 of 75, against 11 of 79 with 25 mg and 7 of 79 with 1 mg); the trial places the suicidal behaviour after week 3, without the one to two months the viewpoint gives; adverse events of any kind affected 66 of 79, 56 of 75 and 57 of 79.
