risk_of_bias.note: Cards sc_goodwin_2022 and sc_raison_2023 (RoB 2, first pass): some concerns overall in both, Raison close to high. Rated very serious here, as the editors rated the MDMA trials for PTSD: in both trials the MADRS, although rated by remote raters who did not know the group, rests on what participants report, and the acute effects of 25 mg very probably let participants tell it from 1 mg or from niacin; neither trial checked blinding or measured expectancy, both sets of authors say blinding was probably weakened, and the Raison authors add that this may have contributed to the effect and to the higher dropout with niacin (9 of 53 against 1 of 51). In Goodwin, new treatment before week 3 was started by 14 of 79 given 1 mg against 4 of 79 given 25 mg, and the later scores of those who started a new antidepressant were imputed by a rule that progressively worsened them (the paper does not say how many of these starts were antidepressants); the alternative analyses said to agree are only in the supplement (not read). Raison's sustained response counts only participants assessed at every visit. All of these run toward a larger difference, of unknown size against differences of 6.6 and 12.3 points. Allocation was concealed centrally in both trials. The sponsors' roles in analysis and interpretation are stated in the claim and not rated twice.

inconsistency.note: Not rated down: both trials favour 25 mg. The size differs (−6.6 points at 3 weeks against a 1-mg dose in treatment-resistant depression; −12.3 at 6 weeks against niacin in mostly non-resistant depression), which population, comparator and time point may explain but two trials cannot test; the claim gives each result separately. In Goodwin 10 mg did not differ from 1 mg; the claim is worded for 25 mg.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: worded for selected trial participants (off antidepressants, without psychotic depression or current suicide risk, mostly White, mostly without recent psychedelic use) given one 25-mg dose with preparation, a supervised session and integration, and for outcomes at 3 and 6 weeks; the statement says that neither trial compared psilocybin with an established treatment or an inert placebo and that the results do not describe use outside such settings.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: each primary interval excludes no difference (−10.2 to −2.9 with 158 participants in the 25-mg and 1-mg groups; −17.5 to −7.2 with 104), and the smaller limit (2.9 points) is given in the statement. Secondary results with wide intervals (sustained response at 12 weeks, odds ratio 0.9 to 5.4; sustained remission, 0.99 to 11.47) are reported as not significant.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from two trials. Both were registered (Goodwin: EudraCT 2017-003288-36 and NCT03775200; Raison: NCT03866174); the registry records were not read. Each was run by the organization that supplied the psilocybin (a company and a non-profit), which interpreted the data; Goodwin reports its failed comparisons. Another single-dose trial in major depression cited by Raison et al. (their reference 15) is not on file.

dose_response.note: Not applicable to randomized evidence; in Goodwin 25 mg differed from 1 mg and 10 mg did not, which the claim reports without using it to rate.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down two levels for risk of bias (participants could very probably tell psilocybin from the control, which neither trial checked, with an outcome that rests on their own answers; the imputation in Goodwin and the uneven dropout in Raison run the same way): low. Rated as worded: larger falls in clinician-rated depression scores 3 weeks (Goodwin, treatment-resistant depression, against a 1-mg dose) and 6 weeks (Raison, mostly non-resistant depression, against niacin) after one 25-mg dose given with psychological support in trials. The claim does not say that the benefit lasts beyond 6 weeks (Goodwin's 12-week sustained response did not differ significantly, and a third of the 25-mg group had started other treatment by then), that 10 mg works (it did not differ from 1 mg), or how psilocybin compares with antidepressants (the separate answer on psilocybin against escitalopram). 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1). The response and remission figures of Goodwin are formally not significant because the testing order stopped at the 10-mg comparison, and Raison's sustained response counts only participants assessed at every visit; both are reported as such. Raison's printed relative incidences for related, mild and moderate adverse events do not fit their counts and are not used. Status replicated: two trials with different sponsors, formulations, populations and lead teams point the same way; they share one site (Emory University, Atlanta) and two of its investigators (B. W. Dunlop; T. Mletzko, listed as Mletzko-Crowe in Goodwin) among 22 and 11 sites, which the editors do not count as the same team; the second reader should confirm. Funding and the authors' ties are given as each paper prints them; Goodwin's disclosure forms are not printed and were not read. One published response to Goodwin et al. is now on file: a two-page viewpoint without data of its own (Gukasyan, 2023), by an author of the Raison trial report who declares a co-investigator role on a psilocybin study funded by the Usona Institute (Raison et al., 2023, pp. 843, 851–852). Its two concerns, the missing blinding check and suicidality, are already in the statement and in the rating (risk of bias down two levels), so it changes neither the certainty nor the status. Its framing was checked against the trial's counts (Goodwin et al., 2022, pp. 1637, 1644–1645): events coded as suicidal behaviour (3 participants after week 3) were all in the 25-mg group, as the viewpoint says, but suicidal ideation or behaviour or self-injury occurred in every dose group, as the trial's abstract states, and worsening of suicidal state by week 3 was most frequent with 10 mg (13 of 75, against 11 of 79 with 25 mg and 7 of 79 with 1 mg); the trial places the suicidal behaviour after week 3, without the one to two months the viewpoint gives, and the viewpoint calls the adverse events relatively high without figures (66 of 79, 56 of 75 and 57 of 79). Published critiques of Raison et al. are not on file; the rating should be revisited when they are (METHODS §2.3).

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether psilocybin given by clinicians with psychological support works better or worse for depression than escitalopram, a common antidepressant (a selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor): only one small head-to-head trial is on file. In that trial, at one London research centre from January 2019 to March 2020, 59 adults with long-standing major depression (a HAM-D-17 score of 17 or more at screening; moderate on average at baseline), most of whom had referred themselves, were randomly assigned to two psilocybin sessions 3 weeks apart with daily placebo capsules (trial conditions: 25 mg of psilocybin on each dosing day; 30 patients) or to 6 weeks of daily escitalopram with two psilocybin sessions at a dose the authors presumed to have negligible activity (trial conditions: escitalopram 10 mg a day for 3 weeks, then 20 mg; psilocybin 1 mg; 29 patients), with the same support from two mental health professionals in both groups (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021). On the primary outcome, a self-rated depression questionnaire (QIDS-SR-16, 0 to 27), scores fell by 8.0 points with psilocybin and 6.0 with escitalopram by week 6, a difference of −2.0 points (95% CI −5.0 to 0.9; P = 0.17), no significant difference; the abstract prints the difference as 2.0, without its minus sign. The interval runs from a moderate advantage for psilocybin to a small advantage for escitalopram, and the trial was neither designed nor large enough to show that the two are equally effective: it was planned with 20 patients per group for 80% power, a size that detects only a difference of about 0.9 standard deviations, about 5 points on this scale (editors' calculation; about 4 points with the 59 enrolled), and no equivalence margin was set. Secondary outcomes mostly favoured psilocybin, but 16 were analysed without correction for multiple comparisons and the authors state that no clinical conclusions can be drawn from them: for example, remission (a score of 5 or less) in 17 of 30 (57 in 100) against 8 of 29 (28 in 100), a difference of 28 percentage points (2 to 54), and response in 21 of 30 (70 in 100) against 14 of 29 (48 in 100), 22 points (−3 to 48). All patients were told that they would receive psilocybin, without the dose; patients given 25 mg rated the acute effects as more intense; blinding was not checked; most patients had referred themselves and many preferred psilocybin; and the primary outcome was rated by the patients themselves, so the authors cannot be confident that guessing or expectations favouring psilocybin did not influence the results. Escitalopram was given for 6 weeks only, which the authors call a limitation because it acts with delay, and 4 of 29 stopped taking it because of adverse events; there was no placebo group, so the trial cannot show how much either treatment did on its own. Adverse events were reported by 26 of 30 (87 in 100) and 24 of 29 (83 in 100), with no serious adverse events; headache was the most common with psilocybin (20 of 30, against 15 of 29), while anxiety and dry mouth (4 of 29 each) occurred only with escitalopram; acute psychedelic effects were not counted as adverse events. The trial was investigator-initiated and funded by a private donation from the Alexander Mosley Charitable Trust and the founding partners of Imperial College London's Centre for Psychedelic Research, with psilocybin supplied by COMPASS Pathways; the first author reports consulting fees from COMPASS Pathways, the Usona Institute and four other organizations, and the last author advisory board fees from COMPASS Pathways, among other ties printed in the paper. Six months on, a follow-up by the trial's own team found no lasting difference in self-rated depression (Erritzoe et al., 2024). It was observational after week 6: there was no further study treatment and no limit on other care, and according to the trial protocol patients were told at the week-6 visit which treatment they had received, which the article does not mention. Depression scores differed between the groups only at month 1 (QIDS-SR-16 −3.58 points, 95% CI −6.31 to −0.85, favouring psilocybin); at month 6 the difference was 1.51 points (−1.35 to 4.38), numerically favouring escitalopram, with both groups improved from the start (−5.27 and −6.83 points); 43 in 100 against 48 in 100 had their score at least halved and 37 in 100 against 34 in 100 were nearly free of symptoms (shares of all randomized patients; the handling of missing data is not stated). By month 6, 25 of 30 and 21 of 29 had returned the questionnaire (at month 3, 9 and 11 were missing, reasons unknown); among those who answered, 8 of 26 and 10 of 23 had taken psychiatric medicines, 12 of 26 and 9 of 22 had had therapy, and 8 of 26 and 4 of 23 had taken psychedelics since the trial (37 of the 59 had some further treatment, about three-quarters of the 49 who answered, editors' calculation); harms were not assessed after week 6. Self-rated work and social functioning, connectedness and meaning in life favoured psilocybin at month 6, ratings made by patients who knew their treatment. In an exploratory analysis of 55 of the patients by the same team (Szigeti et al., 2024), both groups had expected nearly twice as much improvement from psilocybin as from escitalopram before the first dose (estimated means 54 and 28.2 on a 0-to-100 scale); higher expectations went with more improvement in the escitalopram group on four of six scales (not the primary questionnaire), while in the psilocybin group no link was found but one of meaningful size could not be ruled out; adjusted for each patient's expectation of the treatment received, none of the six differences between the groups at week 6 remained significant (without adjustment, three were, after the same correction for multiple tests), though five of the six estimates still favoured psilocybin. A reanalysis by the same team after the primary result was null (Weiss et al., 2023) argued that the primary questionnaire captured the difference less well than the other scales, although its own test found that the questionnaire's compound items did not explain the gap and the authors concede that its larger spread may reflect real differences between patients; on outcomes built afterwards from the items of all the scales, psilocybin did better on depressed mood and on anhedonia (by 0.68 and 0.79 standard deviations) but not on five other groups of symptoms, without correction for multiple tests, results the authors call exploratory. The larger single-dose trial on file had no active comparator, which its authors list as a limitation, calling for comparison with existing treatments (Goodwin et al., 2022). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Only one trial on file has compared psilocybin with an antidepressant. At a London research centre, 59 adults with long-term depression were picked at random for two psilocybin sessions 3 weeks apart, given by clinicians with dummy pills in between, or for 6 weeks of escitalopram pills with two tiny doses of psilocybin; both groups had the same support from two therapists. After 6 weeks, people's own ratings of their depression had fallen by 8 points with psilocybin and by 6 with escitalopram on a 27-point scale, a gap that could be chance. The trial was too small to show that the two work equally well. On many side measures psilocybin did better, for example 57 in 100 against 28 in 100 were nearly free of symptoms, but 16 such measures were tested without allowing for chance findings, and the authors say no firm conclusions can be drawn from them. Everyone was told they would get psilocybin, most had signed up themselves, many preferred psilocybin, and nobody checked whether people could tell what they got. Escitalopram was given for only 6 weeks, though it works slowly, and there was no dummy-only group. Side effects were about as common in both groups; headache was the most common with psilocybin, and anxiety and dry mouth happened only with escitalopram. Six months later, a follow-up by the same team found no lasting difference in depression: 43 in 100 on psilocybin and 48 in 100 on escitalopram had their scores at least halved, and 37 against 34 in 100 were nearly free of symptoms. By then, though, people had been told which treatment they had had, most of those who answered had taken other medicines, therapy or psychedelics, at some monthly checks about 1 in 3 did not answer, and side effects were no longer recorded. Before treatment, people had expected nearly twice as much improvement from psilocybin as from escitalopram; in the team's own exploratory analysis, allowing for these hopes left no clear difference between the groups on any of six scales. Another reanalysis by the team found psilocybin ahead on low mood and on loss of pleasure, using measures built after the main result was known and without allowing for the many comparisons.
population: 59 adults aged 18 to 80 (mean age 41; 20 women; 52 White) with long-standing major depression (HAM-D-17 of 17 or more at screening, with the diagnosis confirmed by the general practitioner; mean illness duration 22.1 and 15.1 years; average baseline severity in the moderate range), most of whom had referred themselves to the trial after hearing about it, seen at one London research centre (NIHR Imperial Clinical Research Facility) from January 2019 to March 2020; psychiatric medicines stopped at least 2 weeks and psychotherapy at least 3 weeks before the first trial medicine; previous escitalopram use excluded, previous psilocybin use allowed (8 of 30 and 8 of 29 had used it, editors' arithmetic from Table 1)
exposure: Two psilocybin sessions 3 weeks apart given by clinicians in the trial, each supervised by the patient's two mental health professionals, with preparation, debriefing and integration, plus daily placebo capsules for 6 weeks (trial conditions: 25 mg of psilocybin on each dosing day); 30 patients
comparator: Escitalopram, a selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor, taken daily for 6 weeks (trial conditions: 10 mg a day for 3 weeks, then 20 mg, with a reduction to 10 mg allowed), with two psilocybin sessions at 1 mg, presumed by the authors to have negligible activity, and the same psychological support; 29 patients; no placebo group
outcome: Change in the self-rated QIDS-SR-16 (0 to 27) from baseline to week 6 (primary); 16 secondary outcomes analysed without correction for multiple comparisons, including QIDS-SR-16 response and remission and the clinician-rated HAM-D-17 and MADRS; adverse events; in the trial team's observational follow-up, the QIDS-SR-16 monthly to month 6 and functioning, connectedness, flourishing and meaning in life every 3 months (Erritzoe et al., 2024)
magnitude: Carhart-Harris et al. (2021), intention to treat (30, 29): QIDS-SR-16 change to week 6, adjusted for baseline, −8.0 (SE 1.0) against −6.0 (SE 1.0), difference −2.0 (95% CI −5.0 to 0.9), P = 0.17 (printed as 2.0 in the abstract). Editors' calculation: standard deviation of change about 5.8 points, back-calculated from the printed interval; observed difference about 0.35 SD (interval from about 0.87 SD favouring psilocybin to about 0.16 SD favouring escitalopram); detectable with 80% power at two-sided 0.05, about 0.89 SD (about 5 points) with the planned 20 per group and about 0.73 SD (about 4 points) with 30 and 29. Secondary, uncorrected for 16 comparisons: response 21/30 (70%) against 14/29 (48%), difference 22 percentage points (−3 to 48); remission 17/30 (57%) against 8/29 (28%), 28 (2 to 54) in Table 2 and 28.1 (2.3 to 53.8) in the text (raw differences 21.7, Wald 95% interval −2.8 to 46.2, and 29.1, 5.0 to 53.1, editors' calculation); HAM-D-17 difference −5.3 (−8.2 to −2.4); MADRS −7.2 (−12.1 to −2.4); BDI-1A −7.6 (−13.3 to −1.8). Adverse events 26/30 (87%) against 24/29 (83%); no serious adverse events; escitalopram stopped because of adverse events by 4/29. Erritzoe et al. (2024), the trial team's observational follow-up (QIDS-SR-16 change from baseline, psilocybin minus escitalopram, mixed model without imputation): week 6 −1.28 (95% CI −3.93 to 1.36; the trial's primary result is −2.0, a difference the paper does not explain); month 1 −3.58 (−6.31 to −0.85; FDR-adjusted p = 0.021); month 6 1.51 (−1.35 to 4.38; p = 0.311); within-group change at month 6 −5.27 and −6.83; at month 6, response 43% against 48% and remission 37% against 34% (shares of all 30 and 29 randomized patients, editors' calculation; Supplementary Table 6); month-6 questionnaire returned by 25/30 and 21/29; other treatment during follow-up among respondents: medication 8/26 against 10/23, therapy 12/26 against 9/22, psychedelics 8/26 against 4/23; month-6 differences favouring psilocybin on the WSAS −7.46 (−12.4 to −2.47), WCS 11.02 (1.25 to 20.83) and MLQ 4.86 (0.67 to 9.05). Szigeti et al. (2024), 55 patients: expectancy 54 against 28.2 (0 to 100; difference 25.8 ± 3.5); between-group differences at week 6 without and with adjustment for expectancy (Bonferroni-adjusted p): HAM-D −6.0 (0.002) and −3.1 (0.438), BDI −7.6 (0.069) and −3.3 (1), MADRS −7.9 (0.013) and −4.5 (0.711), QIDS-SR-16 −1.3 (1) and 0.8 (1), STAI-T −8.2 (0.089) and −3.0 (1), WEMWBS 9.5 (0.01) and 7.8 (0.214). Weiss et al. (2023), post hoc and uncorrected: depressed mood facet −0.68 SD (p = 0.013), anhedonia −0.79 SD (p = 0.001), five other facets not different, single depression factor −0.55 SD (p = 0.035).

evidence.locator: Methods › Trial Oversight, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Patients, 1st paragraph, and 2nd paragraph (p. 1403, continued on p. 1404); Patients, 3rd paragraph (p. 1404)
evidence.extracted: Investigator-initiated, university-sponsored trial with visits at the NIHR Imperial Clinical Research Facility, London, from January 2019 through March 2020. Psilocybin was provided by COMPASS Pathways, and escitalopram and placebo by the Pharmacy Manufacturing Unit at Guy's and St Thomas' Hospital; the first author designed the trial and wrote the first draft; the authors state that there was no industry involvement in data collection or analysis and no agreements between the authors and any commercial entity. Adults aged 18 to 80 were recruited formally through trial networks and informally through social media and other sources that directed them to a recruitment website; information about the trial, including the entry criteria, was made available online on the Centre for Psychedelic Research website, ClinicalTrials.gov, the MQ recruitment platform and the ISRCTN registry; volunteers contacted the recruitment coordinator by email after hearing about the trial, and most patients recruited referred themselves. Entry required a HAM-D-17 score of at least 17, assessed by video call, and a diagnosis of depression confirmed by the general practitioner. Main exclusions: personal or immediate family history of psychosis, serious medical conditions, a history of serious suicide attempts, a positive pregnancy test, contraindications to SSRIs or MRI, previous escitalopram use (previous psilocybin use was allowed), and conditions such as borderline personality disorder judged likely to jeopardize rapport with the two caregivers. Psychiatric medicines were fully stopped at least 2 weeks, and psychotherapy at least 3 weeks, before the first trial medicine. Each patient was assigned two mental health professionals, one of them a clinical psychologist, psychotherapist or psychiatrist, present at all visits.

evidence.extracted: Randomization by random-number generator, implemented by staff outside the research team; six visits over 6 weeks; size- and colour-matched placebo capsules. On dosing-day 1 the psilocybin group received 25 mg of psilocybin and the escitalopram group 1 mg, a dose presumed to have negligible activity; to standardize expectations, all patients were told they would receive psilocybin, without being told the dose; medicines and placebos had non-disclosing labels, and investigators and medication staff did not know the assignments. Each dosing day was supervised by the patient's two mental health professionals, with debriefings afterwards and an integration session after the second dosing day. Daily capsules from dosing-day 1: placebo (microcrystalline cellulose) in the psilocybin group, escitalopram 10 mg in the escitalopram group; 3 weeks later a second dosing day, then two capsules daily (placebo, or escitalopram 20 mg) for 3 more weeks; the primary outcome was assessed at the final visit, at week 6. A placebo group (1 mg psilocybin with placebo capsules) was in the initial design but was dropped as too complex and expensive to conduct and power with the resources available. Primary outcome: change from baseline in the self-rated QIDS-SR-16 (0 to 27) at week 6; secondary outcomes included response (a fall of at least 50%, as defined in Methods) and remission (a score of 0 to 5) at week 6 and changes in the BDI-1A, HAM-D-17 and MADRS. Power: based on earlier trials and on equal variance for the two drugs, 20 patients per group were required for 80% power at two-sided P<0.05 (the difference assumed is not stated), and at least 30 per group were planned; all randomized patients were analysed (intention to treat).

evidence.extracted: The authors describe the sample as having long-standing, mild-to-severe depression (the abstract says moderate-to-severe), with average baseline severity in the moderate range, which limits extrapolation to severe or treatment-resistant depression; scores fell in both groups, but without a placebo group conclusions about the effect of either drug alone are limited. Within-arm change from baseline at month 6, single-arm and uncorrected (panels 1B and 1C): −5.27 (d 1.33) with psilocybin and −6.83 (d 1.35) with escitalopram. At month 6, self-rated work and social functioning (WSAS −7.46, −12.4 to −2.47), connectedness (WCS 11.02, 1.25 to 20.83) and meaning in life (MLQ 4.86, 0.67 to 9.05) favoured psilocybin; flourishing did not differ (Time × Condition F(3,147) = 1.79, p = 0.15). The authors interpret no difference between conditions in antidepressant response, suggest that psychometric problems of the QIDS-SR-16 described by their own team may have contributed to the null result, and state that the study was not optimally powered to detect small but meaningful differences (p. 13); they call the absence of a systematic assessment of side effects during follow-up a limitation (p. 14). Editors' note: the week-6 estimate of this model (−1.28) differs from the trial's primary result (−2.0, 95% CI −5.0 to 0.9), which the paper does not explain.

evidence.locator: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Methods › Baseline measures, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDF p. 2); Results › Pre-treatment between-group differences, 1st paragraph, and Figure 1 (PDF p. 3); Results › Within-treatment-arm association between expectancy and therapeutic outcomes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, and Figure 2 (PDF p. 4); Results › Within-treatment-arm association among suggestibility, absorption, and therapeutic outcomes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 4, 2nd continued on p. 5); Results › Between-treatment difference in models adjusted for expectancy and suggestibility, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 5); Discussion, 6th paragraph (PDF p. 6); Limitations and future work, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDF p. 7); the 59 randomized from the trial report (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021, p. 1402)
evidence.extracted: Exploratory analysis by the trial's own team (five of the six authors at Imperial College London's Centre for Psychedelic Research, and the trial's first author, at the University of California San Francisco), not pre-registered, of 55 patients (28 escitalopram, 27 psilocybin); the trial randomized 59 (per the trial report), and the article does not say why four were not analysed. The day before the first dosing day, patients rated on a 0–100 scale, with one unvalidated item for each treatment, how much improvement in their mental health they expected from 6 weeks of daily escitalopram and from two full strong doses of psilocybin. Irrespective of allocation, expectancy was higher for psilocybin: difference 25.8 ± 3.5 points, p < 0.001, estimated means 54 and 28.2. In the escitalopram arm, higher expectancy for escitalopram went with more improvement at week 6 on the HAM-D (−3.91 ± 0.9 points per standard deviation of expectancy, about 22 points; Bonferroni-adjusted p = 0.001), BDI (adjusted p = 0.013), MADRS (0.022) and STAI-T (0.028), but not on the QIDS-SR-16 (0.115) or WEMWBS (0.641). In the psilocybin arm, psilocybin expectancy was not associated with improvement on any scale (all adjusted p = 1), and equivalence tests were not significant, so an association as large as 0.5 standardized mean difference could not be ruled out. Adjusted for the expectancy for the treatment received, no between-arm difference was significant: HAM-D −3.06 ± 1.67 (adjusted p = 0.438), BDI −3.32 ± 3.49 (1), MADRS −4.52 ± 2.85 (0.711), QIDS-SR-16 0.82 ± 1.93 (1), STAI-T −3.03 ± 3.92 (1), WEMWBS 7.82 ± 3.61 (0.214); five of the six estimates favour psilocybin. Higher baseline suggestibility went with more improvement in the psilocybin arm on all six scales and in the escitalopram arm on none. The abstract concludes that psychedelic therapy may be less vulnerable to expectancy biases than previously suspected; the Discussion reads the contrast between the adjusted and unadjusted results as implying that the expectancy imbalance biased the trial's results in favour of psilocybin, through low expectancy in the escitalopram arm. Limitations stated by the authors: an exploratory and correlational analysis, an unvalidated expectancy measure, a trial not powered to exclude the minimum important difference, and no allocation-guess data from patients or assessors, so blinding integrity could not be evaluated.

evidence.extracted: Post hoc psychometric reanalysis of the trial's baseline and week-6 data (QIDS-SR-16 also at week 5) by the trial's own team (all five authors at Imperial College London's Centre for Psychedelic Research, the trial's first author also at the University of California San Francisco), motivated by the null result of the pre-registered primary outcome, the QIDS-SR-16, while 14 of 16 efficacy outcomes favoured psilocybin; the authors call the analyses exploratory and note their risk of false positives. Significance threshold p < 0.05, two-tailed; no correction for multiple tests is described. On seven depression facets built afterwards by allocating items of five scales to a published factor structure (derived in 119 people and not confirmed), psilocybin therapy improved more than escitalopram on depressed mood (standardized difference −0.68, p = 0.013) and anhedonia (−0.79, p = 0.001), with no significant difference on amotivation, negative cognition, reduced appetite, impaired sleep or suicidal thoughts; on a single depression factor derived in the same 57 patients, −0.55 (p = 0.035). The facet differences are reported as present when relative expectancy is controlled for (models in the supplement, not read). The authors' own test found that removing the QIDS-SR-16's compound criteria did not meaningfully alter its between-arm estimate, and they state that its higher variance could equally reflect greater precision in capturing real variation between patients; clinicians' expectancies were not measured, and the baseline internal consistency of the HAM-D in this trial was α 0.15. Supported by a private donation from the Alexander Mosley Charitable Trust and by the founding partners of Imperial College London's Centre for Psychedelic Research, the funders also named in the trial report; the analysis was designed and conducted by the first author. Editors' calculation: with a Bonferroni threshold for the eight composite outcomes (0.05/8, about 0.006), only the anhedonia facet would remain significant.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_carhart_harris_2021 (RoB 2, first pass): high overall, from the measurement domain. The primary outcome is self-rated by patients who were told they would receive psilocybin, who could probably tell 25 mg from 1 mg (they rated the acute effects as more intense), who had mostly referred themselves and in many cases preferred psilocybin, with no blinding check; the authors cannot be confident that guessing or expectations did not influence the results. Exposure to the comparator was reduced (4 of 29 stopped escitalopram, 1 halved it). These biases run toward psilocybin, so the true difference on the primary outcome may be smaller than −2.0 points. Randomization was done by staff outside the research team; few data were missing, although the number with a week-6 score is not stated. Companion papers (cards sc_erritzoe_2024, sc_szigeti_2024 and sc_weiss_2023, first pass, each high overall): after week 6 the comparison is open (allocation disclosed at the week-6 visit, according to the protocol), with uncontrolled other treatment and self-rated outcomes; before the first dose patients expected nearly twice as much improvement from psilocybin as from escitalopram (54 against 28.2 out of 100), which supports the judgement that expectations favoured psilocybin.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for a 6-week course of escitalopram given with two 1-mg psilocybin sessions and the same psychological support, in a self-selected and moderately depressed sample, and states that the authors call the short course a limitation.

imprecision.note: Very serious: 59 patients; the interval for the primary difference (−5.0 to 0.9 points) includes a moderate advantage for psilocybin and a small one for escitalopram; the trial was planned with 20 per group for 80% power, which detects only about 0.89 standard deviations (editors' calculation), and was not designed for equivalence or noninferiority, so neither a difference nor its absence is shown with precision. At month 6 of the follow-up (25 and 21 respondents) the difference was 1.51 points (−1.35 to 4.38), again compatible with a difference in either direction.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one trial; registered (NCT03429075); the registry record was not read, and the protocol (versions 5 and 7, in the supplement of Erritzoe et al., 2024) only at the passages on unblinding and on the purpose of the follow-up.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down two levels for risk of bias and two for imprecision: very low, the floor. The relation is insufficient evidence (METHODS §6.1, §6.3): the primary result does not show a difference, and with 59 patients and no prespecified margin it cannot show that psilocybin and escitalopram are equally effective; a non-significant P value is not evidence of no difference. The secondary results favouring psilocybin are uncorrected for 16 comparisons and are the ones most exposed to expectancy, so they are reported as the authors frame them and not used for the answer. The sign of the primary difference is taken from the Results and Table 2 (−2.0), not from the abstract (2.0). The comparison lasted 6 weeks and had no placebo group, so it cannot show the effect of either drug alone. Status single study: no other head-to-head trial is on file, and the larger single-dose trial had no active comparator (Goodwin et al., 2022); the 6-month follow-up and the two secondary analyses use the same patients and are counted with the trial, not as replication (METHODS §6.3, overlapping evidence). Funding and ties are given as printed; the disclosure forms were not read. Companion papers of 12 November, all by the trial's own team and none an independent critique: the 6-month follow-up (Erritzoe et al., 2024) is observational after week 6, with patients told their allocation at the week-6 visit according to the protocol (the article calls it a follow-up of a double-blind trial and does not say so), other treatment uncontrolled and recorded only as yes or no at month 6 (about three-quarters of those who answered had some, editors' calculation from 37 of 49), up to 11 of 29 missing at a time point, self-rated outcomes, and harms, which the protocol planned to follow, not assessed; at high risk of bias and imprecise (month 6, 1.51 points, −1.35 to 4.38), it shows no lasting difference in self-rated depression and changes neither the relation nor the certainty, which is already at the floor. Its secondary outcomes favouring psilocybin (functioning, connectedness, meaning in life) were rated by patients who knew their allocation and are reported, not used for the answer. The expectancy analysis (Szigeti et al., 2024) bears on the risk-of-bias judgement: patients expected nearly twice as much improvement from psilocybin, and adjusting for expectation left no between-group difference significant; because the expectation entered for each patient refers to the treatment received, it differs between the groups by design, so the adjusted comparison does not by itself show that the differences were due to expectation (editors' reading, as on the card). The questionnaire reanalysis (Weiss et al., 2023) defines its outcomes after the primary result was known and corrects for no multiple tests, so its facet results are reported as the authors frame them (exploratory) and not used for the answer; with a Bonferroni threshold for its eight composite outcomes (0.05/8, about 0.006), only the anhedonia facet (p = 0.001) would remain significant (editors' calculation). Independent published critiques of the trial are still not on file; the rating should be revisited when they are (METHODS §2.3). The editors' calculations (the standard deviation back-calculated from the printed interval and the detectable differences) are for the second reader to recompute.

statement: In 36 healthy volunteers in Baltimore who had never used hallucinogens and who all took part at least now and then in religious or spiritual activities (Griffiths et al., 2006; 20 daily and 14 at least monthly; mean age 46; 14 men; 35 college graduates; recruited with community flyers about a study of states of consciousness and a substance used sacramentally in some cultures, and unpaid), psilocybin given by the study under supportive conditions (trial conditions: a capsule of 30 mg/70 kg by mouth in an 8-hour session alone with two monitors in a living-room-like room, lying down with an eye mask and classical music, after four preparation meetings of 8 hours in all whose stated expectation was that sessions could increase personal awareness and insight), compared within the same people with methylphenidate (40 mg/70 kg), a stimulant chosen as an active comparison, the two sessions given 2 months apart in random order to 30 of them (15 per order), is associated with much higher scores on questionnaires of mystical experience about 7 hours after the capsule, and 2 months later with higher self-rated personal meaning, spiritual significance and well-being that the volunteers attributed to the session, a small positive change rated by people who knew them, and no detectable difference on personality or mood questionnaires. 'Mystical' here means questionnaire scores: on the 43-item Pahnke–Richards Mystical Experience Questionnaire, part of a 100-item questionnaire and based on Stace's descriptions of mystical experience, the seven scales (internal and external unity, transcendence of time and space, ineffability, sacredness, intuitive knowledge and deeply felt positive mood) averaged 0.66 to 0.81 of the maximum after psilocybin against 0.21 to 0.38 after methylphenidate, and the 32-item Mysticism Scale total was 252.1 against 174.7 (all P < 0.001; means with standard errors, no intervals). A 'complete' mystical experience was defined in advance as at least 0.6 of the maximum on each of six scales: 19 of the 30 met it in their blinded psilocybin session (10 of 15 in the first session and 9 of 15 in the second; 63 in 100, editors' sum), and the paper's headline figure, 22 of 36 (61%), adds 3 of the 6 decoy volunteers whose third session was open-label psilocybin; 4 of 36 met it after methylphenidate (2 in each of the first two sessions, which included the decoy volunteers' two methylphenidate sessions). The questionnaire on lasting effects, assembled for this study from earlier and new items and introduced after it had begun, was completed by 24 of the 30 (12 per order): 2 months after psilocybin, 16 of 24 (67 in 100) rated it the single most meaningful experience of their lives (3) or among the top five (13) (counts from Figure 3, editors' reading), against 2 of 24 after methylphenidate (top five; none the single most), and some likened its meaning to the birth of a first child or the death of a parent; 33% (8 of 24) rated it the single most spiritually significant experience of their lives and another 38% (9) among the top five, against 8% (2) after methylphenidate; 79% (19) said it had increased their well-being or life satisfaction moderately (50%) or very much (29%), against 17% (4) and 4% (1) after methylphenidate, and no one reported a decrease after either drug (counts out of 24 by editors' arithmetic). Mean ratings were 6.54 against 3.42 for personal meaning (1 to 8), 4.79 against 2.63 for spiritual significance (1 to 6) and +2.04 against +0.79 for change in well-being (−3 to +3) (each P < 0.001). Three adults named by each participant (relatives, friends or colleagues), interviewed by telephone 7 to 8 weeks after each session and told their own earlier ratings, rated a mean positive change of 2.42 after psilocybin against −0.03 after methylphenidate (26 participants analysed; P < 0.01), which the authors call small. The NEO PI-R personality inventory and the PANAS-X positive and negative affect scales showed no difference attributable to psilocybin (no values shown); lifetime mysticism and spiritual transcendence scores were higher after psilocybin, shown only in a figure without numbers. The experience was not uniformly pleasant: monitors rated higher peak anxiety or fearfulness during psilocybin sessions (1.05 against 0.42 on a 0 to 4 scale) as well as more joy (2.03 against 0.63) and peace (1.90 against 0.92); 11 of 36 volunteers rated their fear during the psilocybin session as strong or extreme (none after methylphenidate); 8 of 36 had a period of notable anxiety or dysphoria, 4 of them for the whole session (6 of the 30 in blinded sessions, editors' count), and 6 of these 8 had transient ideas of reference or paranoid thinking; these were managed with reassurance, no volunteer needed drug treatment, 2 compared the experience to being in a war and 3 said they would never want to repeat it, while most of the 8 still rated it as meaningful. The authors, who call this 31% with significant fear and 17% with transient ideas of reference or paranoia, warn that without monitoring such reactions could escalate to panic and dangerous behaviour. Participants and monitors were told that at least one session would bring a moderate or high dose of psilocybin; participants were never asked which drug they thought they had received; the monitors misclassified 23% of sessions (the primary monitor 17%), mostly by calling methylphenidate psilocybin, and the authors judged the blinding adequately maintained because the monitors still believed several drugs and placebo had been given. Three of the four commentaries published with the trial in the same issue, none with data of its own, read the monitors' errors in about a quarter of sessions as a sign of careful blinding (Kleber, 2006) or of results unlikely to reflect expectations (Snyder, 2006), or the stimulant comparison as showing effects beyond expectation (Schuster, 2006), although the participants themselves were never asked. The authors state that how far the results generalize is unknown and that the volunteers' religious or spiritual interest may have made a spiritually significant reading of the experience more likely. In a separate randomized trial by another team, in 93 adults with alcohol dependence who were not selected for religious or spiritual practice (Bogenschutz et al., 2022; funded by the Heffter Research Institute, an NIH translational-science grant and private donors), mean total scores on the same 43-item questionnaire (0 to 1) were 0.59 after a first psilocybin session (25 mg/70 kg) against 0.10 after the antihistamine diphenhydramine as an active placebo, and 0.64 against 0.11 after the second session (both P < .001), with correct guesses of the medication after about 94 in 100 sessions (percentages without counts). Griffiths et al. was funded by the US National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Council on Spiritual Practices, which two of its four authors list as an affiliation, and prints no conflict-of-interest statement. The 2-month ratings come from one study; its 1-year follow-up, under way in 2006, is reported only as bringing no mention of persisting perceptual effects or problematic recreational hallucinogen use in open interviews with 30 of 36. Certainty: low. Status: replicated for the questionnaire scores during the session (two independent trials); the 2-month ratings rest on one study.
plain: In a study at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, 30 healthy volunteers who had never tried psychedelics, and who all took part in religious or spiritual activities, were given psilocybin once and a stimulant (methylphenidate) once, 2 months apart and in random order, in calm, supported 8-hour sessions. Here 'mystical' meant high scores on questionnaires about feelings such as unity, sacredness and timelessness: 19 of the 30 scored high enough on psilocybin to count as a 'complete' mystical experience, and a few people did after the stimulant. Two months later, 16 of 24 (about 2 in 3) ranked the psilocybin session among the 5 most meaningful experiences of their lives, against 2 of 24 for the stimulant, and most said it had made their lives better; people close to them rated small positive changes, but personality and mood questionnaires did not change. It was not all calm: 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they would never want to repeat it. The volunteers were never asked which drug they thought they got, and the authors say their religious or spiritual interest may have made a spiritual reading more likely. Another team's trial, in 93 people with drinking problems, also found high questionnaire scores during psilocybin sessions, but almost everyone there guessed which pill they had. The lasting part comes from one study.
population: 36 healthy, hallucinogen-naive adults in Baltimore (mean age 46, range 24 to 64; 14 men; 35 college graduates, 20 with postgraduate degrees) who all reported at least intermittent participation in religious or spiritual activities (20 daily, 14 at least monthly), recruited by community flyers and unpaid, 30 of them in the blinded crossover (Griffiths et al., 2006); and, for the questionnaire scores during the session only, 93 treated adults aged 25 to 65 with DSM-IV alcohol dependence in a randomized trial at two US academic centres, 2014 to 2020 (Bogenschutz et al., 2022)
exposure: Psilocybin given by the study in individual 8-hour sessions under supportive conditions (trial conditions: 30 mg/70 kg by mouth after about 8 hours of preparation meetings, with two monitors, eye mask and music, in Griffiths et al.; 25 mg/70 kg, then 30 or 40 mg/70 kg, by mouth within 12 psychotherapy sessions in Bogenschutz et al.)
comparator: Methylphenidate hydrochloride 40 mg/70 kg by mouth, an active stimulant, in the same people 2 months apart in random order (Griffiths et al.); diphenhydramine 50 mg, then 100 mg, as an active placebo in a parallel group with the same psychotherapy (Bogenschutz et al.)
outcome: Mystical-experience questionnaire scores about 7 hours after the capsule (the 43-item Pahnke–Richards Mystical Experience Questionnaire within the States of Consciousness Questionnaire; the 32-item Mysticism Scale) and a predefined 'complete' mystical experience; 2 months later, self-rated personal meaning, spiritual significance and change in well-being or life satisfaction, ratings by three people who knew each participant, personality (NEO PI-R), affect (PANAS-X) and lifetime mysticism scores; fear, anxiety and ideas of reference during sessions
magnitude: Griffiths et al. (2006), within-person, N=30, means (SEM): Mysticism Scale total 252.1 (8.5) against 174.7 (11.3); States of Consciousness Questionnaire scales 0.66 to 0.81 against 0.21 to 0.38 of the maximum; all P < 0.001, no intervals printed. Complete mystical experience: 19 of 30 in blinded psilocybin sessions (editors' sum of 10 of 15 and 9 of 15; exact 95% interval 44% to 80%, editors' calculation); 22 of 36 including 3 of 6 open-label sessions; 4 of 36 after methylphenidate. At 2 months (N=24): single most or top-five most meaningful 16 of 24 (67%; exact 95% interval 45% to 84%, editors' calculation) against 2 of 24; single most spiritually significant 33%, top five another 38%, against 8% top five; well-being increased moderately or very much 79% against 21% (17% and 4%); mean personal meaning 6.54 (0.22) against 3.42 (0.35), spiritual significance 4.79 (0.26) against 2.63 (0.22), change in well-being +2.04 (0.17) against +0.79 (0.18), each P < 0.001. Observers (N=26): mean positive change 2.42 (0.70) against −0.03 (0.68), P < 0.01. NEO PI-R and PANAS-X: no difference, values not shown. Strong or extreme fear 11 of 36 against none; notable anxiety or dysphoria 8 of 36 (6 of 30 in blinded sessions, editors' count). Bogenschutz et al. (2022), 48 against 45: mean MEQ total 0.59 (SD 0.24) against 0.10 (0.13) after session 1 and 0.64 (0.21) against 0.11 (0.16) after session 2, P < .001; correct guesses after 93.6% and 94.7% of sessions.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 268); Materials and methods › Participants, and Study design, 1st paragraph (p. 269, continued on p. 270)
evidence.extracted: Double-blind study at Johns Hopkins (Baltimore) of psilocybin against methylphenidate in hallucinogen-naive adults reporting regular participation in religious or spiritual activities. Recruited from the local community through flyers announcing a study of states of consciousness brought about by a naturally occurring psychoactive substance used sacramentally in some cultures; 135 screened by telephone and 54 in person; 36 enrolled (14 men), medically and psychiatrically healthy, with no history of hallucinogen use and no family history of psychotic or bipolar I or II disorder; mean age 46 (range 24 to 64); 35 (97%) college graduates and 20 (56%) with postgraduate degrees; 30 employed full time; 19 affiliated with a religious or spiritual community (both shares printed in words); all 36 reported at least intermittent participation in religious or spiritual activities such as services, prayer or meditation, 20 (56%) daily and 14 (39%) at least monthly; no monetary compensation; their motivation was described as curiosity about psilocybin and the chance for self-reflection. Design: 36 randomly assigned to two sessions (N=30) or three (N=6), 8 hours each and 2 months apart; the 30 randomly assigned to psilocybin or methylphenidate first (15 per group), with the other drug in the second session; the 6 received methylphenidate in the first two sessions and unblinded psilocybin in a third, a condition meant mainly to obscure the design, and their data were not used in the statistical analyses. Questionnaires about 7 hours after the capsule and 2 months after each session; measures of psychiatric symptoms and quality of life are listed among the longitudinal measures (p. 270), but no results for them are reported.

evidence.locator: Materials and methods › Drug conditions; Meetings with monitor before and after sessions; Drug sessions; Instructions to participants and monitors (begins p. 270, continues p. 271)
evidence.extracted: Trial conditions: psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg and methylphenidate hydrochloride 40 mg/70 kg by mouth in identical opaque capsules with about 180 ml of water; the authors chose the psilocybin dose as a high dose they judged safe from studies of the 1950s and 1960s, and the methylphenidate dose as high and discriminable, with an onset and duration like psilocybin's and some overlapping effects (excitability, nervousness, raised positive mood). The primary monitor, a clinical psychologist experienced in hallucinogen sessions, met each participant four times (8 hours in all) before the first session and four times (4 hours) after each session; the preparation explicitly included the monitor's expectation that sessions could increase personal awareness and insight, but avoided mentioning the criteria for mystical experience. Sessions: a urine sample to verify drug-free status; 8 hours in a living-room-like room with two monitors; participants encouraged to lie on a couch with an eye mask and headphones playing the same classical music programme for everyone, and to focus on their inner experience; monitors gave verbal or physical reassurance (a supportive touch to the hand or shoulder) when a participant reported significant fear or anxiety. Participants and monitors were told that participants would have two or three sessions, that at least one would bring a moderate or high dose of psilocybin, and that other sessions might bring an inactive placebo, a low dose of psilocybin or one of 11 other drugs; after the data collection 2 months after the second session, the 6 decoy participants were told their third session would bring psilocybin, so these 6 sessions were the only unblinded ones.

evidence.locator: Materials and methods › Measures assessed 7 h after drug administration › States of consciousness questionnaire (begins p. 271, continues p. 272) and Mysticism scale (p. 272)
evidence.extracted: About 7 hours after the capsule, when the main drug effects had subsided, participants completed three questionnaires on drug effects and two on mystical experience. The 100-item States of Consciousness Questionnaire is rated from 0 (none) to 5 (extreme, more than ever before in one's life); forty-three of its items (printed in words) form the Pahnke–Richards Mystical Experience Questionnaire, used as a primary outcome of the Good Friday Experiment (Pahnke, 1963) and based on Stace's descriptive work on mystical experience, with seven scales: internal unity, external unity, transcendence of time and space, ineffability and paradoxicality, sacredness, noetic quality and deeply felt positive mood, each expressed as a proportion of the maximum possible score; the other 57 items were distracters. Criteria set in advance, after Pahnke, for a 'complete' mystical experience: a score of at least 0.6 on each of unity (internal or external, whichever higher), transcendence of time and space, ineffability, sacredness, noetic quality and positive mood. The 32-item Mysticism Scale (rated −4 to +4), well regarded in the psychology of religion, had not previously been used to assess changes after a drug experience.

evidence.extracted: The authors state that how far the study population limits the generalizability of the results is unknown: the participants were hallucinogen-naive, well educated, psychologically stable, middle-aged adults reporting regular religious or spiritual activities, whose religious or spiritual interest plausibly may have increased the likelihood that the experience would be interpreted as having substantial spiritual significance and personal meaning, and the novelty of the experience for hallucinogen-naive people may also have enhanced its intensity and significance. Overall, 23% of sessions were misclassified by one or both monitors (methylphenidate identified as psilocybin, or psilocybin as something else); the primary monitor's rate was 17%, and most errors were methylphenidate sessions rated as psilocybin; on two of the three occasions when the primary monitor rated a psilocybin session as something else, the participant later rated the experience among the five most meaningful and spiritually significant of their life. At the end, both monitors believed that a range of psilocybin doses, other active drugs and placebo had been given, and the primary monitor guessed that methylphenidate had not been used; the authors conclude that the blinding was adequately maintained despite the drugs' different profiles. risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_griffiths_2006 (RoB 2, first pass): overall high, from outcome measurement. Every outcome except blood pressure and heart rate is a rating by the participant or by monitors who were present; participants were told that at least one session would bring psilocybin and were never asked to guess, the monitors recognized most psilocybin sessions, and the preparation conveyed an expectation that sessions could increase awareness and insight; the 2-month outcomes are the volunteers' attributions of change, from a questionnaire introduced after the study began (24 of 30). In the second trial (card sc_bogenschutz_2022, RoB 2 high), participants guessed their medication correctly after about 94 in 100 sessions. Down one level, not two: the acute differences are large (scales at 0.66 to 0.81 of the maximum against 0.21 to 0.38), were seen against an active stimulant and again in a second trial, and a self-rating is how meaning and mystical experience are defined.

inconsistency.note: The two trials agree on the direction of the acute questionnaire effect; the 2-month ratings come from one study, so their consistency cannot be judged.

indirectness.note: Not rated down because the claim is worded for what was studied: 'mystical' as questionnaire scores, volunteers selected for religious or spiritual practice, a supportive setting with preparation and two monitors, and 2 months of follow-up. It is not worded for people who take psilocybin outside research, and the plain lines say who took part.

imprecision.note: The 2-month ratings rest on 24 people in one study, with no intervals printed (16 of 24 ranking it among the five most meaningful experiences has an exact 95% interval of 45% to 84%, editors' calculation); the acute contrast rests on 30 people within one study, with only P thresholds printed, and on 93 in the second trial.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from two studies; no registration is mentioned for Griffiths et al.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence (a crossover with drug order assigned at random, and a parallel-group trial) starts high; down one level for risk of bias (self-rated outcomes, expectation, functional unblinding) and one for imprecision (24 people for the 2-month ratings): low. Rated as worded: much higher scores on mystical-experience questionnaires after psilocybin than after an active comparison, and, 2 months later, in volunteers selected for religious or spiritual practice, higher self-rated meaning and attributed change, a small change rated by people who knew them and no detectable change on personality or mood inventories; it does not say that psilocybin changes personality or that most people who take it have a mystical experience. 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1). Status replicated for the acute questionnaire effect only: Griffiths et al. (Johns Hopkins, against methylphenidate) and Bogenschutz et al. (New York University and the University of New Mexico, against diphenhydramine) are independent; the 2-month ratings, the comparison with a stimulant and the counts of 'complete' mystical experiences rest on Griffiths et al. alone, and the plain lines say 'one study' for them. The paper's headline counts pool the 30 blinded volunteers with 6 open-label sessions (22 of 36 complete mystical experiences, 11 of 36 strong fear, 8 of 36 notable anxiety); the claim gives the blinded count (19 of 30) beside them. Not used: the 14-month follow-up of these volunteers (Griffiths et al., 2008), known here only as cited by Johnson et al. (2014). The four commentaries published with the paper in the same issue (Nichols, 2006; Snyder, 2006; Schuster, 2006; Kleber, 2006), the published responses METHODS §2.3 asks for, have now been read in full: all four praise the trial and none reports data of its own, so they enter only as what they argue and change neither the certainty nor the replication status. Snyder, Kleber and Schuster treated expectation as controlled, from the monitors' errors or the stimulant comparison; participants were never asked to guess, and the risk-of-bias downgrade already counts this. Schuster also argued that the expectations set by the preparation and the introspective setting may be an important determinant of the experience, which the claim's wording for supportive conditions already reflects. The only harm figure in the four, Kleber's 8 of 36 volunteers with sessions dominated by anxiety or dysphoria, is the trial's own; Snyder calls adverse events very few, without numbers. Nichols, who synthesized the trial's psilocybin (Griffiths et al., 2006, p. 282), calls the trial placebo-controlled, although its comparison was an active drug; he is not entered. Funding and the funder affiliation of two authors are stated. No doses are given beyond the trial conditions.

statement: In adults with DSM-IV alcohol dependence who were not in treatment and had no major psychiatric or other drug use disorder, recruited through local media at two US academic centres (University of New Mexico, 2014 to 2015; New York University, 2015 to 2020) (Bogenschutz et al., 2022; 95 randomized, 93 treated and analysed; mean age 46; 42 of 95 women; 75 of 95 non-Hispanic White; median household income $100 000; in the 12 weeks before screening, drinking on 74.9% of days and heavily on 52.7%), psilocybin given by clinicians in two 8-hour sessions within 12 sessions of psychotherapy (motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy from a team of two therapists including a psychiatrist; trial conditions: 25 mg/70 kg by mouth at week 4, then 30 or 40 mg/70 kg at week 8), compared with diphenhydramine (an antihistamine) as an active placebo with the same psychotherapy (50 mg, then 100 mg), is associated with fewer self-reported heavy drinking days (5 or more drinks in a day for men, 4 or more for women) over the 32 weeks (8 months) after the first dose: 9.71% of days with psilocybin (48 people) against 23.57% with diphenhydramine (45), a difference of 13.86 percentage points (95% CI 3.00 to 24.72; Hedges g 0.52, 0.11 to 0.94), so that heavy drinking days in the psilocybin group were 41% of those in the diphenhydramine group. The Methods give the prespecified primary window as weeks 5 to 32, while the abstract, results, tables and figure use weeks 5 to 36, the 32-week double-blind period; the registry record and protocol were not read. Both groups had already cut heavy drinking sharply before any medication, during 4 weeks of psychotherapy while trying to stop drinking: from 56.48% to 24.11% of days in those later given psilocybin and from 48.57% to 21.31% in those later given diphenhydramine (decreases of 32.37 points, 95% CI 23.68 to 41.07, and 27.26, 20.83 to 33.69), so both groups more than halved their heavy drinking days before the first dose, about two-thirds of the psilocybin group's fall from screening to the follow-up mean came before it, and the diphenhydramine group's follow-up mean was close to its level in the 4 weeks before dosing (editors' arithmetic; the paper does not say whether its follow-up means are observed or model estimates). Participants guessed their medication correctly after 93.6% of first and 94.7% of second medication sessions, and therapists after 92.4% and 97.4% (percentages without the numbers of guesses); the authors name the failure of diphenhydramine to keep the blind as their first limitation and say biased expectancies could have influenced the results. Drinking was reported by the participants in timeline follow-back interviews; a hair or fingernail alcohol marker (EtG) at week 24 was available for 50 of 93 and was negative in all 14 who reported total abstinence. Exploratory secondary outcomes, without correction for multiple comparisons: drinks per day 1.17 against 2.26 (difference 1.09, 0.27 to 1.92); no heavy drinking days at all in the 32 weeks, 16 of 48 against 5 of 45 (odds ratio 4, 1.32 to 12.10); no drinking at all, 11 of 48 against 4 of 45 (odds ratio 3.05, 0.89 to 10.40); in the final month, no drinking 23 of 48 against 11 of 45. There were no serious adverse events with psilocybin and three, all during binge drinking, with diphenhydramine; within 48 hours of dosing, headache occurred in 21 of 48 against 2 of 45, and two people given psilocybin received a sedative for anxiety during their second session. Enrolment stopped at 95 of up to 180 planned when COVID-19 halted recruitment; the authors state that participants drank less intensely at screening than in most medication trials for alcohol use disorder, that the two-group design cannot separate the effect of the psychotherapy, and that effects beyond 32 weeks are unknown. Funding: the Heffter Research Institute, which reviewed and approved the protocol, an NIH translational-science grant and individual donors; the first author is named as inventor on a provisional patent application related to this work filed by his employer, with his rights waived, the employer licensed commercial rights to the trial data to B.More, Inc for a nominal sum, and a co-author reported two patents issued by Reset Pharmaceuticals. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In one trial at two US universities, 93 adults with alcohol use disorder were offered 12 sessions of talk therapy, and chance decided whether they also got psilocybin twice or a comparison pill (diphenhydramine). Over the next 8 months, people given psilocybin reported heavy drinking on about 10 in 100 days, against 24 in 100 days for the comparison pill. Heavy drinking had already more than halved in both groups during the first 4 weeks of therapy, before any pill. After about 94 in 100 sessions people guessed correctly which pill they had had, and they reported their own drinking, so expectations may explain part of the difference; the trial was also smaller than planned and lasted 8 months.
population: Adults aged 25 to 65 with DSM-IV alcohol dependence and at least 4 heavy drinking days in the 30 days before screening, not in treatment, without major psychiatric or other drug use disorders and with no hallucinogen use in the past year or more than 25 lifetime uses, recruited through local media at two US academic centres, 2014 to 2020 (95 randomized, 93 treated; mean age 45.8; 42 women; 75 non-Hispanic White; Bogenschutz et al., 2022)
exposure: Psilocybin given by clinicians within structured psychotherapy: two 8-hour sessions (trial conditions: 25 mg/70 kg, then 30 or 40 mg/70 kg, by mouth) within 12 sessions of motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy
comparator: Diphenhydramine as an active placebo (50 mg, then 100 mg) with the same psychotherapy, allocated at random
outcome: Percentage of heavy drinking days over the 32 weeks after the first dose, from timeline follow-back interviews (primary); drinks per day and other exploratory drinking outcomes; guesses of the medication; adverse events
magnitude: Bogenschutz et al. (2022), 48 against 45: heavy drinking days 9.71% against 23.57% over weeks 5 to 36, difference 13.86 percentage points (95% CI 3.00 to 24.72), Hedges g 0.52 (0.11 to 0.94), P = .01, decomposed from a multivariate test across three drinking outcomes (F1,86 = 6.18, P = .02); before any medication, decreases of 32.37 (23.68 to 41.07) and 27.26 (20.83 to 33.69) points from screening to the 4 weeks before dosing; drinks per day 1.17 against 2.26, difference 1.09 (0.27 to 1.92); no heavy drinking days 16/48 against 5/45, odds ratio 4 (1.32 to 12.10); no drinking in weeks 5 to 36 11/48 against 4/45, odds ratio 3.05 (0.89 to 10.40); no drinking in weeks 33 to 36 23/48 against 11/45, odds ratio 2.84 (1.17 to 6.89); correct guesses after 93.6% and 94.7% of sessions (participants) and 92.4% and 97.4% (therapists); headache within 48 hours 21/48 against 2/45; serious adverse events 0 against 3.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 953); Methods › Trial Oversight; Participants; Trial Design › Overview; Psychotherapeutic Elements of Treatment (p. 954)
evidence.extracted: Double-blind randomized trial at two US academic centres (University of New Mexico and New York University), registered as NCT02061293; participants recruited from the community through advertisements in local media from March 12, 2014, to May 13, 2015 (New Mexico) and from July 9, 2015, to March 19, 2020 (New York). Eligible: aged 25 to 65, DSM-IV alcohol dependence by structured clinical interview, at least 4 heavy drinking days (5 or more drinks in a day for a man, 4 or more for a woman) in the 30 days before screening; excluded: major psychiatric and drug use disorders, any hallucinogen use in the past year or more than 25 lifetime uses, medical contraindications to either medication, exclusionary medications and current treatment for alcohol use disorder. Randomized 1:1 to psilocybin or diphenhydramine in two 8-hour sessions at weeks 4 and 8, within 12 psychotherapy sessions (4 before the first medication session, 4 between the two and 4 in the month after the second) from a team of 2 therapists including a licensed psychiatrist, combining motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy with material on managing and using the medication's effects (the abstract names motivational enhancement therapy); double-blind observation over weeks 5 to 36, after which an open-label psilocybin session was offered at week 38 (not reported here). Participants were paid up to $560 for completing assessments, not for therapy or medication sessions. Psilocybin was provided by the Usona Institute, Nicholas Cozzi and David Nichols; the first author held the investigational new drug application.

evidence.locator: Methods › Randomization and Blinding; Dosage of Study Medication; Administration of Study Medication; Outcomes and Assessments › Drinking Outcomes; Safety and Blinding Integrity; Statistical Analysis › Sample Size and Power; Subjective Effects and Efficacy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Randomization stratified by site in balanced blocks of varying size, the sequence generated and treatment assigned by a pharmacist at each site; all other staff and the participants blinded. Trial conditions: one opaque capsule of unvarying appearance by mouth; psilocybin 25 mg/70 kg or diphenhydramine 50 mg in the first session; in the second, if there were no dose-limiting adverse events and the participant agreed, psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg (first-session MEQ total 0.6 or more) or 40 mg/70 kg (less than 0.6), or diphenhydramine 100 mg; at least 8 hours in the session room with the therapists, lying on a couch with eyeshades and headphones playing a standardized playlist; medications for hypertension, severe anxiety or psychotic symptoms on hand. The primary outcome is stated as the percentage of heavy drinking days during weeks 5 to 32, assessed at weeks 8, 12, 24 and 36 by timeline follow-back (one standard drink, 14 g of ethanol); secondary outcomes were drinking days, drinks per day, abstinence, no heavy drinking days and falls in WHO risk level; hair or fingernail EtG at week 24 to confirm reported abstinence. After each session participants and therapists guessed the medication and rated their certainty from 0 to 100. Planned to randomize up to 180, with a sample-size re-estimate after 100; enrolment halted at 95 when COVID-19 suspended recruitment on March 19, 2020. Multivariate repeated-measures analysis of the three continuous drinking outcomes over monthly bins listed as weeks 5 to 8 through 29 to 32 and 32 to 36, adjusted for each outcome in weeks 1 to 4, with missing months imputed; no correction for multiple comparisons, so analyses of secondary outcomes are described as exploratory.

evidence.extracted: In the 32 weeks after the first dose, 204 adverse events were reported (119 in the psilocybin group, 85 in the diphenhydramine group). risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_bogenschutz_2022 (RoB 2, checked by a second reader and adjudicated): overall high, from outcome measurement. Drinking was self-reported in timeline follow-back interviews by participants who guessed their medication correctly after 93.6% and 94.7% of sessions (p. 957), with a biochemical check for only 50 of 93 at one time point (negative in all 14 who reported abstinence); more people given diphenhydramine declined the second session (10 of 45 against 4 of 48); the primary window is stated as weeks 5 to 32 in the Methods and 5 to 36 elsewhere. Randomization (site-stratified blocks assigned by a pharmacist), retention (96.4% of participant-months) and the analysis of all treated participants are sound. Down one level.

inconsistency.note: One randomized trial, so consistency cannot be judged.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for the trial's population (DSM-IV alcohol dependence, lower drinking intensity than in most medication trials, no major psychiatric comorbidity, not in treatment), its setting (12 psychotherapy sessions, two therapists including a psychiatrist, careful screening) and its 32 weeks.

imprecision.note: 93 people; the interval for the difference in heavy drinking days runs from 3.00 to 24.72 percentage points, from a small to a large effect; enrolment stopped at 95 of up to 180 planned; the interval for no drinking at all includes no difference (odds ratio 0.89 to 10.40).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one trial; registered as NCT02061293, but the registry record and the protocol were not read, so registered and reported outcomes were not compared.

grade.reasoning: Rated on one randomized trial: randomized evidence starts high; down one level for risk of bias (self-reported drinking by participants who almost all knew their allocation) and one for imprecision (93 people, an interval from 3.00 to 24.72 points, a trial stopped early): low. 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1). Status single study: one trial, not replicated among the sources read. The fall in the psilocybin group's heavy drinking days from screening to follow-up (56.48% to 9.71%, an 83% fall by editors' arithmetic) is not used as an effect: most of it came before any medication, in both groups. No doses are given beyond the trial conditions, and the sedative given for anxiety is named without its dose. The smoking pilot this answer used to include is now a separate answer, rated on its own evidence (very low), because GRADE rates certainty per outcome.
