statement: In adults who smoked at least 10 cigarettes a day and still wanted to quit after several attempts, evidence is insufficient to say whether psilocybin given by a study team within an intensive counselling programme, compared with the same programme without psilocybin (not studied: there was no comparison group), changes how many stop smoking: in one open-label pilot at Johns Hopkins (Johnson et al., 2014), 15 adults (10 men; mean age 51; 14 White) who smoked a mean of 19 cigarettes a day for 31 years and had a mean of 6 earlier quit attempts, recruited through advertisements offering a smoking-cessation treatment involving psilocybin (323 screened by telephone, 27 in person) and unpaid, received a 15-week programme of cognitive behavioural therapy with preparation for the sessions (19 in-person meetings and daily calls for 2 weeks after the quit date), with psilocybin given by the study team on the quit date in week 5, in week 7 and optionally in week 13 (trial conditions: 20 mg/70 kg first, then 30 mg/70 kg by default; the route is not stated in this paper). At 6 months, 12 of 15 (80 in 100; exact 95% interval 52% to 96%, editors' calculation) had not smoked in the previous 7 days by their own report, confirmed by breath carbon monoxide and urine cotinine; 3 of these 12 reported lapses of 1, 4 and 48 cigarettes and a fourth a relapse before stopping again, so the paper reports no smoking after the quit date for 8 of 15 (editors' count; continuous abstinence is not reported as such), and the 3 who did not quit resumed daily smoking after 4, 11 and 22 days. The abstract says this rate substantially exceeds the rates commonly reported for other treatments (typically under 35%). The Discussion compares it with 24.9% to 26.3% (bupropion) and 33.5% to 35.2% (varenicline) in trials with 12 brief counselling meetings and with 17.2% for the counselling programme its own was based on, noting that its participants had substantially more staff contact, and with 45% to 59% at about 6 months in two trials of extended treatment combining bupropion, nicotine replacement and cognitive behavioural therapy, saying its rate was higher; the authors say the results should be interpreted with caution, that no definitive conclusions can be drawn about psilocybin's causal role and that the sample's racial homogeneity and high education may have affected the outcomes, and they call for a randomized trial. With an interval of 52% to 96%, the pilot cannot show that its programme did better than intensive standard treatment, and without a comparison group it cannot separate psilocybin from the counselling, contact and motivation of volunteers who sought out a psilocybin treatment (editors' reading). During the 42 sessions, no clinically significant adverse event needed a physician or medication; 6 of 15 rated fear, fear of insanity or feeling trapped as strong or extreme at some point, all resolved by the end of the session. Funding: the Beckley Foundation and the Heffter Research Institute, on whose board of directors one author sits. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study at Johns Hopkins, 15 adults who had smoked for 31 years on average got psilocybin two or three times within 15 weeks of intensive counselling. Six months later, 12 of the 15 (80 in 100) were not smoking, confirmed by breath and urine tests, though 4 of those 12 had smoked again at some point before stopping again. There was no comparison group, so the study cannot show what psilocybin added to the counselling, and the paper's own discussion cites 45 to 59 in 100 not smoking after intensive standard treatment in other trials. So it is not known whether psilocybin helps people stop smoking.
population: Adults who smoked at least 10 cigarettes a day, had made several unsuccessful quit attempts and still wanted to quit, were healthy on screening and had no personal or family history of psychotic or bipolar disorder and no drug dependence other than nicotine in the past 5 years, and who answered advertisements for a psilocybin smoking-cessation treatment at Johns Hopkins (15 enrolled of 323 screened by telephone; 10 men; mean age 51; 14 White; a mean of 19 cigarettes a day for 31 years and 6 earlier quit attempts; Johnson et al., 2014)
exposure: Psilocybin given by the study team in two or three sessions (trial conditions: 20 mg/70 kg on the quit date in week 5, then 30 mg/70 kg by default in week 7 and optionally in week 13, with the lower dose allowed; the route is not stated in this paper; 42 sessions in all) within a 15-week cognitive behavioural smoking-cessation programme with preparation for the sessions, 19 in-person meetings and brief daily calls for 2 weeks after the quit date; participants were told not to use other cessation treatments
comparator: None: the pilot had no comparison group; the authors compare their result with published trials of other treatments in other people (bupropion or varenicline with brief counselling, the counselling programme theirs was based on, and extended treatment combining bupropion, nicotine replacement and cognitive behavioural therapy)
outcome: 7-day point-prevalence abstinence 6 months after the quit date, from timeline follow-back calendars confirmed by breath carbon monoxide (6 ppm or less) and urine cotinine (below 200 ng/mL); lapses (any smoking after the quit date) and relapses (smoking on 7 or more consecutive days); adverse events during the sessions
magnitude: Johnson et al. (2014), 15 people, no comparison group, so no difference between groups can be estimated: 7-day point-prevalence abstinence at 6 months 12/15 (80%; exact 95% interval 51.9% to 95.7%, editors' calculation), self-reported and confirmed by breath carbon monoxide and urine cotinine; lapses of 1, 4 and 48 cigarettes in 3 of the 12 and a relapse in a fourth, leaving 8/15 with no smoking reported after the quit date (editors' count); the 3 who did not quit resumed daily smoking after 4, 11 and 22 days; strong or extreme ratings of fear, fear of insanity or feeling trapped at some point 6/15; no clinically significant adverse event needing a physician or medication in 42 sessions. Rates the Discussion cites from other trials in other people, at about 6 months: 45% to 59% with extended combined treatment, 33.5% to 35.2% with varenicline and 24.9% to 26.3% with bupropion (with 12 brief counselling meetings), and 17.2% with the counselling programme its own was based on.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 983); Introduction, 3rd paragraph (begins p. 983, continues p. 984); Table 1; Methods, 1st paragraph; Participants; Procedures, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (p. 984)
evidence.extracted: Open-label pilot at Johns Hopkins, conducted without a control condition as a first step to evaluate safety and whether results would justify a randomized trial. Recruited through advertisements offering a novel smoking-cessation treatment involving psilocybin: 323 screened by telephone (those excluded mainly seeking payment, taking medications or smoking too little), 27 in person, 15 enrolled (10 men), all of whom completed the study; no monetary compensation. Inclusion: at least 10 cigarettes a day, healthy, several unsuccessful quit attempts, still wanting to quit; excluded: personal or family history of psychotic or bipolar disorder, and drug dependence (including alcohol, excluding nicotine) in the past 5 years. Table 1 (N=15): age 51 (SD 10.5, range 26 to 65); Fagerström dependence score 5.3; 31 years of smoking; 6 previous quit attempts; 19 cigarettes a day at intake (range 15 to 25); 14 (93%) White and one Asian; ten reported minimal past hallucinogen use (mean 8 lifetime uses, the most recent a mean of 27 years before intake) and five none. Programme: 15 weeks, with four weekly preparation meetings combining cognitive behavioural therapy for smoking cessation with preparation for the sessions; the target quit date coincided with the first psilocybin session in week 5, with further sessions in week 7 and optionally week 13; weekly support meetings, 19 in-person meetings in all, and brief daily calls for 2 weeks after the quit date; participants were told not to use other cessation treatments. Trial conditions: psilocybin 20 mg/70 kg in the first session and 30 mg/70 kg by default in the later ones, with the lower dose allowed; the route is not stated in this paper, whose sessions were conducted as previously described (Griffiths et al., 2006, 2011).

evidence.extracted: By timeline follow-back verified by breath carbon monoxide and cotinine, 12 of 15 (80%) showed seven-day point-prevalence abstinence at the 6-month follow-up. Eleven of the 12 reported quitting on the quit date and were biologically verified abstinent through the following 10 weeks of treatment; the twelfth reported quitting on the quit date and was verified abstinent at every meeting attended but had to leave the country for business, so had no third session and gave no samples for weeks 6 to 10 after the quit date. All 12 who quit did so after the first, lower-dose session, and the 3 who did not quit could not do so after the later sessions either. Editors' count: lapses or a relapse were reported for 4 of the 12, leaving 8 of 15 with no smoking reported after the quit date; continuous abstinence is not reported as an outcome. risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_johnson_2014 (ROBINS-I, checked by a second reader and adjudicated): overall critical, from confounding. The pilot was run without a control condition (pp. 983–984), so whatever psilocybin contributed cannot be separated from the cognitive behavioural therapy, the 19 in-person meetings and daily calls, the motivation and expectations of volunteers who answered an advertisement for a psilocybin treatment, or the passage of time. Selection of participants, deviations from the intended programme, outcome measurement and selection of the reported result are judged moderate: abstinence at 6 months was confirmed by breath carbon monoxide and urine cotinine, which protects the main outcome; no registration is mentioned, and the reported measure, 7-day point prevalence, is more favourable than continuous abstinence. Down two levels.

inconsistency.note: One study, so consistency cannot be judged.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the answer is worded for the pilot's population (15 screened volunteers, almost all White and highly educated, who answered an advertisement for a psilocybin treatment), its intensive programme and its 6-month follow-up.

imprecision.note: 15 people: the exact 95% interval for 12 of 15 runs from 52% to 96% (editors' calculation; p. 988), wide enough to include the 45% to 59% that the Discussion cites for extended combined treatment in other trials (p. 990). Down one level.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one study; the paper mentions no registration, and registries were not searched.

large_effect.note: Not applied: with no comparison group there is no effect estimate to rate; the comparison with other trials' rates is across different people and programmes.

grade.reasoning: Rated on one open-label pilot without a comparison group (Johnson et al., 2014): non-randomized evidence starts low; down two levels for risk of bias (critical: psilocybin came with intensive counselling and staff contact in volunteers who sought out a psilocybin treatment, and nothing was compared) and one for imprecision (15 people; an interval from 52% to 96%): very low, the lowest level, which either reason alone would reach. 'Evidence is insufficient' because without a comparison there is no estimate of what psilocybin did (METHODS §6.1): the 12 of 15 is reported as what happened to 15 volunteers, not as an effect. The abstract's comparison with other treatments (typically under 35%) is not adopted, because it sets the pilot against other trials in other people with less staff contact, and the Discussion's own figures for extended combined treatment (45% to 59%) fall within the pilot's interval. Status single study: no controlled test of psilocybin for smoking was among the sources read (card sc_johnson_2014). Split from the answer on drinking, which rests on a randomized trial and is rated low on its own, because GRADE rates certainty per outcome. No doses are given beyond the trial conditions.

statement: In adults who were already planning to microdose, microdoses compared with identical-looking dummy capsules are associated with higher self-rated drug effects on the days they were taken but not with any detected benefit on mood, well-being, creativity, thinking or daily activity, in two randomized studies by independent teams: a trial of psilocybin mushrooms alone (34 people, two capsules in one week) and a larger self-blinding study of people's own psychedelic, three in four of them LSD or an LSD-like drug (240 people, 4 weeks), in which small same-day differences in mood, energy and creativity ratings, and in end-of-week anxiety, disappeared when each person's guess of what they had taken was taken into account. In the first, 34 adults in Buenos Aires (11 women; mean age 31; on average 11 earlier experiences with psychedelics, and only 6 with significant earlier microdosing experience; recruited by word of mouth, social media and microdosing workshops from December 2019 to August 2020, unpaid; told in writing before consenting why a dummy condition was needed, and screened by an interview that excluded people with psychotic, bipolar, depressive, obsessive-compulsive, generalized anxiety, panic or eating disorders, a substance use disorder in the past 5 years, a neurological disorder or any psychiatric medication) took, double-blind, one week of two capsules of ground dried Psilocybe cubensis mushroom (study condition: 0.5 g of dried mushroom per capsule, taken on a Wednesday and a Friday) and one week of identical capsules of an edible mushroom; each participant drew one of two identical coded envelopes to set the order, and a third party held the code until the data had been analysed (the article says the third party randomized the order), but how many people had each order is not reported, so effects of order cannot be checked (Cavanna et al., 2022; funded by Argentine and Czech public research grants; the authors declare no competing interests). The summed rating of 21 acute-effect items was higher with the mushroom on both dosing days (about 66 against 39 on the Wednesday and 61 against 40 on the Friday, by the supplement's Table S1) and not on the days after; split by each person's own guess of what they had taken, the difference was clear in weeks with a correct guess (25 mushroom and 24 dummy weeks) and inconclusive in weeks with a wrong guess (9 and 10 weeks), and no single item survived correction for 21 tests. Dummy weeks that people took for mushroom weeks were rated higher on the dosing days than dummy weeks they identified correctly (43 and 53 against 37 and 35, by the supplement's Table S2), and mushroom weeks taken for dummy weeks lower than mushroom weeks identified correctly (59 and 52 against 68 and 64); this fits expectation shaping the ratings as well as felt effects shaping the guesses, and the paper reports no test of it. Ten questionnaires on the second dosing day (state anxiety, positive and negative feelings, stress, absorption, well-being, mind-wandering, flow, creative personality, empathy and mental flexibility) did not differ on paired tests (most Bayes factors as printed favoured no difference, though by the editors' recalculation they ignore the pairing of the two weeks within each person); two trait measures taken before each week's first capsule, conscientiousness and (shown only in the supplement) suggestibility, differed at uncorrected thresholds only, which cannot reflect that week's capsules; two scores from three creativity tests differed at an uncorrected threshold, none after correction (by the supplement, fewer ideas on the Alternative Uses Task and more elaboration on the Wallach–Kogan test with the mushroom); three task measures (an attention task, reaction times on the Stroop test and time on a trail-making test) were worse with the mushroom, two at uncorrected thresholds only and the third with no correction stated; wristband steps, distance, resting and activity time did not differ; and with eyes closed, EEG power in the theta band was lower, surviving correction for the four bands reported (a fifth, gamma, was computed but not reported). People guessed correctly whether they had taken mushroom or dummy capsules in 49 of 68 measurement weeks (72 in 100, editors' calculation from the counts in Fig. 1d; the text gives 49 of 64 weeks, 75%), where guessing at random would be right about half the time: a statistical test did not show better-than-chance guessing after the first week but did after the second, which, the authors say, could indicate that knowing the first week's condition helped. Participants' expectations were collected in 17 areas but not analysed; no primary outcome was named and no power calculation made; the supplement gives means and p-values but no effect sizes or confidence intervals, and none at all for the tasks, EEG or wristband; and the trial gave two doses in one week, whereas microdosing, the authors note, usually goes on for longer. In the second, run online from Imperial College London without clinical supervision (Szigeti et al., 2021), 240 adults with psychedelic experience who planned to microdose with their own substance (147 LSD, 33 LSD-like drugs, 57 psilocybin mushrooms and 3 other, amounts and contents unverified; recruited on online and offline forums, unpaid, with no health screening described; mean age 33.5; 74 in 100 called themselves active advocates of psychedelic drug use) packed their microdoses and identical empty capsules (for mushrooms, capsules of a non-psychoactive mushroom) into coded envelopes and, by a constrained random draw, took 4 weeks of dummy capsules (78 people), 2 weeks of each (71) or 4 weeks with two microdoses a week among the dummies (91); 191 completed the week-5 primary endpoint and 159 an optional week-9 follow-up. Well-being, mindfulness, life satisfaction and paranoia scores improved from the start in the microdose group, and mindfulness and paranoia also improved in the dummy group, but no group difference was significant at week 5 or week 9 on these scales, the personality traits or a cognitive score (well-being 2.5 points higher with microdoses, 95% CI −3.1 to 8.1, editors' calculation from the printed 2.5 ± 5.6); the LSD and mushroom groups are said to match the combined results, without numbers. On capsule days, microdoses were rated as more intense (12.5 points on a 0-to-100 scale; standardized difference 0.58) and slightly better on positive feelings, mood, energy and creativity (0.19 to 0.27), and weeks with microdoses were followed by slightly lower trait-anxiety scores. People guessed the day's capsule correctly on 72 of 100 capsule days on average, against about 62 for someone guessing from the known three-to-one share of dummy capsules; they named microdose on 45 of 100 microdose days, and people taking only dummies named microdose on 21 of 100 capsule days. With each guess added to the analyses, only felt intensity still differed (3.4 points), and with the capsule held fixed, scores were better when people believed they had taken a microdose in 21 of 22 comparisons; the cognitive score followed neither. Because the guesses were asked after the ratings, these analyses cannot show whether belief raised the ratings or feeling something produced the guess, as the authors note. Every group took capsules, so there was no untreated group: the study cannot separate a placebo response from improvement that would have come anyway, with time, retesting or regression toward the average, and its abstract's conclusion that the anecdotal benefits are explained by the placebo effect goes beyond what this design can show. The authors estimate that 1392 to 4918 participants would have been needed for 90% power on the questionnaires; the Funding section declares no external funding, while the Acknowledgements thank the Beckley Foundation for funds; no competing interests are declared. Neither study tested people with depression or other conditions, or microdosing over months. Certainty: low. Status: replicated (two independent studies; only the smaller tested psilocybin mushrooms alone).
plain: Two trials compared microdoses with look-alike dummy capsules in people who were about to start microdosing. In Argentina, 34 people took two capsules of dried magic mushroom (psilocybin mushroom) in one week and two capsules of an ordinary edible mushroom in another, without knowing which was which. In a larger study run from London, 240 people mixed their own microdoses, mostly LSD and about a quarter magic mushrooms, with empty capsules, and a random draw decided who had 4 weeks of dummies, 2 weeks of each or 4 weeks with microdoses. In both, people rated stronger drug effects on microdose days, but mood, well-being, creativity and thinking were no better than with dummies, and after 4 weeks the dummy-only group was not clearly worse off; small same-day lifts in mood and energy in the larger study disappeared once people's guesses were taken into account. People guessed right about 7 times in 10, and their ratings followed what they believed they had taken, though the guesses came after the ratings. No group took nothing at all, so neither study can say how much was a placebo effect and how much would have changed anyway, and neither tested months of microdosing or people with depression.
population: Adults planning to microdose, in two studies. Cavanna et al. (2022): 34 adults (11 women; mean age 31.26, SD 4.41) in Buenos Aires, Argentina, recruited from December 2019 to August 2020 by word of mouth, social media advertising and visits to workshops on psilocybin mushrooms and microdosing, who were planning to start microdosing with their own Psilocybe cubensis and agreed to the study's standardized schedule and dose; on average 11 (SD 14.9) earlier experiences with serotonergic psychedelics, 1.5 (SD 2.3) of them challenging; only 6 with significant earlier microdosing experience; fluent Spanish speakers with normal or corrected vision; unpaid; all completed every part of the study; per the supplement, briefed by phone and in writing (including why a blinded placebo condition was needed) and screened by a non-diagnostic psychiatric interview that excluded psychotic or bipolar disorders (also in first- or second-degree relatives), depressive, obsessive-compulsive, generalized anxiety, panic and eating disorders, dysthymia, a substance use disorder in the past 5 years (nicotine excepted), neurological disorders and any psychiatric medication; asked to abstain from psychoactive drugs, including alcohol and caffeine, during the study weeks (adherence not checked). Szigeti et al. (2021): 240 adults at baseline (of 1630 who signed up and 246 who started) with earlier psychedelic experience who intended to microdose with their own psychedelic, recruited through online and offline forums, unpaid, with no health screening described; mean age 33.5 (SD 9.4); 70% men, 19% women and 1% other, as printed (summing to 90%); 33% with a past and 7% with a current psychiatric diagnosis; 74% agreed that they were active advocates of psychedelic drug use; mean baseline expectation of microdosing 68 (SD 19) on a 0-to-100 scale; 191 completed the week-5 primary endpoint and 159 the optional week-9 follow-up.
exposure: Cavanna et al.: one measurement week in which an oral gel capsule of ground, homogenized dried Psilocybe cubensis mushroom was taken on the Wednesday and again on the Friday (study condition: 0.5 g of dried mushroom per capsule; mushrooms from three sources, analysed only as a pooled sample, so the psilocybin content may have varied between participants). Szigeti et al.: the participant's own psychedelic in opaque capsules (vials for liquids), self-sourced and unverified (LSD 147, LSD analogues 33, psilocybin mushrooms 57, other 3), at the amount each person would use outside the study; capsules on four days a week for 4 weeks, two of them microdoses in each microdose week, so 0, 4 or 8 microdoses in all by group (study conditions).
comparator: Cavanna et al.: in the same people, one measurement week of identical capsules holding the same weight of a dried edible mushroom (for example Suillus granulatus) prepared the same way; the order set by each participant's random pick of one of two identical coded envelopes, the third party in charge of blinding holding the key until the data had been collected, scored and analysed (supplement; the article says the third party randomized the order); numbers per order not reported; a week without measurements between the two weeks. Szigeti et al.: identical-looking empty capsules (for people microdosing with mushrooms, capsules of the same weight of a non-psychoactive mushroom), assigned by a constrained random draw of coded envelopes to 4 dummy weeks (78 people), 2 dummy and 2 microdose weeks (71) or 4 microdose weeks with dummy capsules on the other capsule days (91); for the same-day and end-of-week measures, scores on dummy days and after dummy weeks. Neither study had a group without capsules.
outcome: Cavanna et al.: summed self-ratings of 21 acute-effect items, Wednesday to Saturday; ten state questionnaires on the second dosing day and three trait measures before each week's first capsule; three creativity tests; six computer tasks of perception and thinking; resting EEG and auditory event-related potentials; daily wristband activity; each person's guess of their condition after each week; no primary outcome named. Szigeti et al.: well-being (Ryff scales), mindfulness, life satisfaction, paranoia, personality and a cognitive score from six online tasks at baseline, week 5 (primary endpoint) and week 9; on capsule days, positive and negative feelings, six 0-to-100 ratings (drug intensity, mood, energy, creativity, focus, temper) and the cognitive score; at the end of each week, well-being (Warwick–Edinburgh), depressive symptoms, trait anxiety and social connectedness; a guess of the day's capsule and of the week's type, asked after the assessments.
magnitude: Cavanna et al. (2022): no effect sizes or confidence intervals in the article or its supplement (means ± SEM, p-values and BF10 in Supplementary Tables S1–S4, for the acute-effect totals, questionnaires and creativity tests only). Summed acute-effect rating, all weeks (Table S1): Wednesday 65.52 ± 5.84 with mushroom against 38.97 ± 2.95 with dummy (p = 7e-5), Friday 60.55 ± 4.30 against 40.05 ± 3.48 (p = 9e-5), Thursday and Saturday no difference (p = 0.83 and 0.58); correct-guess weeks (Fig. 1d: 25 mushroom, 24 dummy; Table S2) 67.88 against 37.29 (p = 0.0002) and 63.72 against 34.75 (p = 2e-6), Bonferroni-corrected over 4 days, BF10 > 30; wrong-guess weeks (9 and 10) 59.00 against 43.00 (p = 0.16) and 51.77 against 52.80 (p = 0.83), BF10 0.70 and 0.40 (the editors' earlier reading of Fig. 1d, about 68 against 37, 64 against 35, 59 against 43 and 52 against 53, agrees). Questionnaires (Table S1): all p ≥ 0.10 except two trait measures taken before each week's first capsule, conscientiousness 29.76 against 28.14 (p = 0.01) and suggestibility 3.34 against 3.02 (p = 0.03; not named in the article), neither after Bonferroni; 15 of 18 BF10 below 1/3 as printed. Creativity (Table S3): Alternative Uses fluency lower with mushroom, 8.76 against 9.52 (p = 0.03, BF10 0.34), and Wallach–Kogan elaboration higher, 0.02 against 0.01 (p = 0.04, BF10 1.28), neither after Bonferroni; other scores p ≥ 0.22. Editors' recalculation: the printed BF10 values match a Bayes factor for two independent groups of 34 computed from the printed means and SEMs in 7 of 9 rows checked (for example 0.25 for identical means, where 34 pairs would give 0.18; 0.34 for Alternative Uses fluency, where a paired test at p = 0.03 gives about 1.7), the exceptions being conscientiousness and the Wednesday total, so they do not use the within-person pairing that the p-values use. Tasks: attentional-blink second-target visibility at a 300 ms lag lower and Stroop response times longer (p < 0.05 uncorrected, BF10 > 1); trail-making part A time longer. EEG: eyes-closed theta power lower (p < 0.05, Bonferroni over the 4 bands reported; exact p not given; a fifth band, gamma, 30–40 Hz, computed in the Methods but not reported); Lempel-Ziv complexity and auditory ERPs unchanged. Wristband: no differences. Correct guesses: 49 of 68 weeks, 72% (editors' calculation from Fig. 1d), against 49 of 64, 75%, in the text; mushroom weeks 25 of 34 (73.5%); dummy weeks 70% in the text (24 of 34, 70.6%, editors' calculation); chi-square 0.09 (1 df), p = 0.76, after the first week and 11.53, p = 0.0006, after the second. Szigeti et al. (2021): dummy against microdose group at week 5, adjusted difference ± 95% CI half-width: well-being (Ryff) 2.5 ± 5.6 (p = 0.37; −3.1 to 8.1, editors' calculation), mindfulness 0.8 ± 1.5 (p = 0.32), paranoia −1.6 ± 2.5 (p = 0.21), life satisfaction 0.4 ± 1.7 (p = 0.67), personality traits −0.3 to 0.8 (all p ≥ 0.24); no significant between-group difference at week 5 or week 9 except lower paired-associates scores in the half-half group (−0.55 ± 0.43). evidence.extracted: Participants: 34 people (11 women; mean age 31.26, SD 4.41; weight 74, SD 17 kg) recruited by word of mouth, social media advertising and visits to workshops on psilocybin mushrooms and microdosing between December 2019 and August 2020, who were planning to start a microdosing protocol with their own mushroom material and adapted their schedule and dose to the study's standardized conditions; on average 11 (SD 14.9) previous experiences with serotonergic psychedelics, 1.5 (SD 2.3) of them challenging; only 6 reported significant earlier microdosing experience; all fluent in Spanish with normal or corrected vision, and all completed every part of the study; no payment; approved by the ethics committee of the Universidad Abierta Interamericana; stated as registered at ClinicalTrials.gov before it started (NCT05160220; registry record not read). evidence.locator: Materials and methods › Design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, and Outcomes (p. 3); Self-blinding setup procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, and Figure 1 (p. 4); Microdose preparation (single paragraph, p. 5); Figure 2, and Blind breaking and collection of guess data (single paragraph) (p. 6); Appendix 1 › Daily effects of microdosing VASs (p. 20) and Additional information on the self-blinding setup and data collection, 2nd paragraph (p. 22)
evidence.extracted: A self-blinding study run online without clinical supervision: people who planned to microdose with their own psychedelic put microdoses into opaque capsules and prepared identical-looking empty capsules (for mushrooms, capsules of the same weight of a non-psychoactive mushroom, chaga recommended; for liquids, vials), packed weekly sets with QR codes into envelopes and drew four of eight envelopes by a constrained random procedure that assigned each person, with probability 1/3, to 4 dummy weeks (PL), 2 dummy and 2 microdose weeks (HH) or 4 microdose weeks (MD); capsules were taken on four days a week, two of them microdoses in each microdose week, so 0, 4 or 8 microdoses in all (study conditions; each person used the amount they would use outside the study). Scanning the QR codes let only the researchers decode which capsule was taken when. Measures: well-being, mindfulness, life satisfaction, paranoia, personality and a cognitive score at baseline, week 5 (primary endpoint) and an optional week 9; on one capsule day a week, positive and negative feelings, six 0-to-100 ratings and the cognitive score; at the end of each week, on a day without capsules, well-being, depressive symptoms, trait anxiety and social connectedness. Participants guessed, as a forced choice, the day's capsule and, at the end of each week, the week's type. All three groups took capsules on the same schedule (Fig. 1), so the study had no group without capsules (editors' reading of the design).

evidence.locator: Materials and methods › Recruitment and inclusion criteria (single paragraph, p. 5); Ethical considerations (single paragraph, p. 7); Results › Demographics, randomization, and completion rate, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 7); Figure 3 (p. 8); Results › Microdoses (single paragraph, p. 8); Accumulative outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 8); Appendix 1 › Attitude toward psychedelics and microdosing (p. 24)
evidence.extracted: Recruited through advertisements on relevant online and offline forums, with sign-up and consent on the study website; no payment. Inclusion: over 18, good English, intention to microdose with psychedelics, earlier psychedelic experience, no other psychedelic use from a week before the start to week 5, willingness to follow the protocol; no health screening is described. Flow (Figure 3): 1630 signed up and 246 started; 4 did not scan their QR codes and 2 withdrew and asked for their data to be deleted, leaving 240 at baseline (PL 78, HH 71, MD 91; the text says 240 started); 191 at week 5 (65, 57 and 69) and 159 at the optional week 9 (53, 44 and 62); completion did not differ by group (p = 0.99). Participants: mean age 33.5 (SD 9.4); 70% male, 19% female and 1% other, as printed (summing to 90%); 74% and 90% agreed or strongly agreed that they were active advocates of psychedelic drug use and of the therapeutic use of psychedelics; 33% reported a past and 7% a current psychiatric diagnosis; mean baseline expectation score for microdosing 68 (SD 19) on a 0-to-100 scale (p. 24). Substances: LSD 147 (61%), LSD analogues 33 (14%), psilocybin-containing mushrooms 57 (24%), other 3. The LSD and psilocybin subgroups were analysed separately and are said to match the combined results, with no numbers given (p. 8; again for the same-day and end-of-week outcomes, p. 10).

evidence.locator: Results › Accumulative outcomes, 2nd paragraph (p. 8, continuing on p. 9) and 3rd paragraph (p. 9); Figure 4 (p. 9); Accumulative outcomes adjusted for number of microdose guesses (single paragraph, p. 9, continuing on p. 10); Discussion › Limitations, 6th paragraph (p. 15)
evidence.extracted: Within groups, baseline to week 5 (adjusted mean ± 95% CI half-width): the MD group improved on well-being (Ryff scales) 4.2 ± 3.9 (p = 0.04), mindfulness 2.4 ± 1.1, life satisfaction 1.2 ± 1.2 (p = 0.04) and paranoia −5.0 ± 1.7, with lower neuroticism and higher openness; the PL group also improved on mindfulness (1.6 ± 1.1) and paranoia (−3.4 ± 1.7), with lower neuroticism, but not on well-being or life satisfaction; the HH group improved on mindfulness and paranoia; the cognitive score did not change in the MD group and fell in the HH group. Between groups: no significant difference at week 5 or week 9 on any scale or subscale, except lower paired-associates scores in the HH group (PL against HH −0.55 ± 0.43). PL against MD at week 5: well-being 2.5 ± 5.6 (p = 0.37; −3.1 to 8.1, editors' calculation), mindfulness 0.8 ± 1.5 (p = 0.32), paranoia −1.6 ± 2.5 (p = 0.21), life satisfaction 0.4 ± 1.7 (p = 0.67), personality traits −0.3 to 0.8 (all p ≥ 0.24); post hoc, adding the number of microdose guesses as a covariate shrank all but two of these further (well-being 0.9 ± 5.7; intellect unchanged at −0.2; extraversion −0.4 ± 1.3, from −0.2). From their data the authors calculate that 90% power at alpha 0.05 would need 1508 participants for well-being, 1638 for mindfulness, 4918 for life satisfaction, 1392 for paranoia and 366 for the cognitive score (p. 15).

evidence.locator: Results › Acute and post-acute outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs, and Association between guess and acute/post-acute outcomes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 10); Table 2 (p. 11); Figure 5 (p. 12); Discussion › Limitations, 4th paragraph (p. 14)
evidence.extracted: Capsule days, microdose against dummy (Table 2; about 857 scores, four capsule days per person; adjusted mean difference ± 95% CI half-width): drug intensity (0 to 100) observed 21.4 against 8.5, adjusted 12.5 ± 3.0 (Cohen's d 0.58); positive minus negative feelings 2.2 ± 1.4 (d 0.19); mood 4.6 ± 2.9 (d 0.20); energy 5.3 ± 2.7 (d 0.27); creativity 4.7 ± 2.6 (d 0.25); focus, temper and the cognitive score did not differ. End of week: trait anxiety lower after microdose weeks, −1.4 ± 1.3 (p = 0.03) in the text and −1.5 ± 1.3 in Table 2 (d −0.04); well-being, depressive symptoms and social connectedness did not differ. With the guess added to the models, condition remained significant only for drug intensity (3.4 ± 2.0); with the guess held fixed, microdose and dummy differed only on drug intensity (7.3 ± 3.1); with the capsule held fixed, scores differed by guess in 21 of 22 comparisons, all favouring a microdose guess (Figure 5); the cognitive score differed by neither. The guess was the last question of each session, after the assessments, and the authors state that their stratified analysis therefore cannot strictly establish that the guess caused the scores (p. 14).

evidence.locator: Results › Blinding integrity, 1st paragraph (p. 10, continuing on p. 11); Discussion › Limitations, 4th paragraph (p. 14); Appendix 1 › Blind breaking cues, and Comparison to random guesser with Appendix 1—table 1 (pp. 25–26)
evidence.extracted: Correct capsule guesses (break blind rate) 0.72 ± 0.18, mean ± SD across participants; a guesser who knew only the three-to-one share of dummy to microdose capsules, evident when preparing them, would score 0.62. By Appendix 1—table 1 (rates over capsule days): microdose named on 0.45 of microdose days (sensitivity; 0.46 on p. 11) and dummy named on 0.82 of dummy days (specificity); the PL group named microdose on 0.21 of its capsule days. In a post-study survey (n = 166), the cues for guessing microdose were body or perceptual sensations only (24%), mostly bodily (31%), equally bodily and mental (22%), mostly mental (19%) or mental only (4%), and 86% said they had been thinking about which capsule they took before being asked; the authors report a technical error in who was invited to the survey (pp. 14, 25).

evidence.locator: Abstract and competing-interests note (p. 1); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 12) and 3rd paragraph (p. 13); Discussion › Limitations, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs (pp. 14–15); Acknowledgements, and Additional information › Funding and Author contributions (p. 16)
evidence.extracted: The abstract states that the same-day and end-of-week differences can be explained by participants breaking blind and that the findings suggest the anecdotal benefits of microdosing can be explained by the placebo effect; the Discussion reads the absence of between-group differences as suggesting that the improvements are not due to the drug's pharmacological action but are explained by the placebo effect (p. 12) and the guess analyses as strongly suggesting that beliefs about the capsules, not their content, determined the differences (p. 13). Every group took capsules, so no comparison with people taking nothing was possible (editors' reading; anchor 17). Limits the authors state: no verification of the nature, purity or amount of the substance (62% sourced on the illicit market, mostly LSD); adherence to the self-blinding setup and the schedule could not be confirmed (three participants who prepared together drew an invalid sequence); mostly healthy participants with high baseline well-being, so a clinical population might differ, although post hoc subsamples with the lowest baseline well-being or highest neuroticism showed no significant differences. Funding: the Funding section states that no external funding was received, while the Acknowledgements thank the Beckley Foundation for providing funds for the study and an author from the Beckley Foundation is credited with funding acquisition (p. 16); the authors declare no competing interests (p. 1).

risk_of_bias.note: Cards sc_cavanna_2022 and sc_szigeti_2021 (RoB 2, first pass): both overall high, from measurement of the outcome: people identified their condition better than chance (49 of 68 weeks in Cavanna et al.; 72 of 100 capsule days in Szigeti et al., against about 62 for a guesser who knew the share of dummy capsules) while rating their own effects, and both studies' splits by guess suggest that the ratings followed what people believed. Cavanna et al. add no primary outcome among 27 measures, correction within some families only, an order drawn by each participant with the numbers per order unreported (supplement), and the text's 64 weeks against the figure's 68; Szigeti et al. add self-sourced, unverified substances and amounts, unconfirmed adherence, a self-run draw that could not be verified, 20 in 100 missing at week 5, no registration, data-driven covariates and post hoc guess analyses. For the absence of benefit, knowing the condition would tend to favour finding benefits, while unverified amounts and missed capsules in Szigeti et al. would dilute a real effect; the tasks, EEG, wristband and cognitive scores are less exposed. Rated down one level, not two, because both used matched dummy capsules with concealed allocation and their main biases run in opposite directions for the null result.

inconsistency.note: Not rated down: the two studies agree on each kind of finding they share (no detected benefit over dummy capsules; higher self-rated drug effects on dosing days; ratings that follow people's guesses).

indirectness.note: Not rated down: worded for what was tested: psilocybin mushrooms alone in one trial (two capsules in one week, from mushrooms of approximately known content) and people's own unverified psychedelic in the other (61 in 100 LSD, 14 LSD-like drugs, 24 psilocybin mushrooms; up to 8 microdoses over 4 weeks), in mostly healthy, experienced people who planned to microdose. The statement says that the second study is mostly about LSD (its mushroom group's results are not given separately) and that neither tested months of use or people with depression or other conditions.

imprecision.note: Cavanna et al.: 34 people, no power calculation, and no effect sizes or confidence intervals in the article or the supplement (Tables S1–S4 give means, SEMs, p-values and Bayes factors for some outcomes only, and by the editors' recalculation the Bayes factors ignore the within-person pairing); the wrong-guess subset (19 weeks) was inconclusive. Szigeti et al.: 191 people at week 5, with intervals that include modest benefits (well-being difference 2.5, 95% CI −3.1 to 8.1, editors' calculation) and the authors' own estimate that 1392 to 4918 participants would be needed for 90% power on the questionnaires. Small benefits or harms cannot be excluded.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for two studies, both of which reported null main results. Cavanna et al. state registration at ClinicalTrials.gov before the study started (NCT05160220; the registry record was not read); Szigeti et al. mention no registration.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence with matched dummy capsules starts high (one within-person trial; one parallel-group study assigned by a self-run random draw); down one level for risk of bias (people identified their condition better than chance while rating their own effects) and one for imprecision (no intervals in one study; intervals that include modest benefits in the other): low. The self-blinding study (Szigeti et al., 2021), added on 13 November, changes the evidence base: it is larger and longer, by an independent team, with the same findings (no detected benefit over dummy capsules; dosing-day ratings that follow people's guesses), so the status moves from single study to replicated. It does not raise the certainty, because it shares the main bias, adds its own (unverified substances and amounts, unconfirmed adherence) and still cannot exclude modest effects; its evidence is mostly about LSD, and the evidence on psilocybin mushrooms alone rests on one trial of two capsules in one week, as the statement says. Rated as worded: higher self-rated acute effects on dosing days, and no detected benefit on the measures; 'is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1); the absence of benefit is stated as not detected, not as shown, because the intervals do not exclude small effects (§6.3). The analyses by guess group days or weeks by each person's own guess, asked after the ratings, so they cannot show whether expectation produced the ratings or felt effects produced the guess; neither study analysed expectation as a cause (Cavanna et al. collected expectations but deferred their analysis; Szigeti et al. tested a baseline expectation score only as a possible covariate), and with no untreated group neither can separate a placebo response from change that would have happened anyway, so the abstracts' conclusions that expectation or the placebo effect explains the anecdotal benefits are reported, not adopted. Cavanna et al.'s text gives 49 of 64 correctly guessed weeks (75%), against the subgroup counts in Fig. 1d (68 weeks, 49 correct, 72%); the figure's counts are used because every participant completed both weeks, the four counts add to 68, and the text's own 25 of 34 mushroom weeks and 70% of dummy weeks (24 of 34) match them, while 49 of 64 would be 76.6%, not 75%. Cavanna et al.'s supplement, read on 13 November, gives the selection criteria, how the order was drawn, the acute-effect means (which match the editors' earlier reading of Fig. 1d), a second pre-dose trait difference and the direction of the two creativity differences; it changes no conclusion. No amount is given beyond the study conditions. Funding: Cavanna et al., Argentine and Czech public research grants, no competing interests declared; Szigeti et al., no external funding declared in the Funding section while the Acknowledgements thank the Beckley Foundation for funds, no competing interests declared. The two studies share no authors and recruited separately.
